column1: # Genesis, scene by scene: chapter, first verse, last verse, title, cast (keys of cast.tsv), god (y: God shown,
# only ever as light), and what the picture shows. Every verse is in one scene. See make_prompts.py.

column7: Seen from just above the water, a vast dark ocean stretches to every horizon beneath a black, starless sky, formless and empty. Low over the face of the deep, a faint shimmering radiance moves like a breath of wind, stirring the still water into long silver ripples, the first quiet movement in a silent, waiting world.

Seen from high above, a brilliant beam of pure light bursts through total darkness and spreads across a vast, still primordial ocean. Half the sky is still black and half glows gold, and the glassy water mirrors both, the first day and the first night meeting at the horizon in awe-filled silence.

Seen from the surface of a boundless sea, a great expanse of clear blue sky opens overhead, lifting a ceiling of heavy grey waters and cloud high above the waves. Radiant shafts of light pour through the widening gap, mist rises from the sea, and the bright new heaven stretches between the waters above and the waters below.

At dawn, seen from high above, the seas roll back in vast foaming torrents as bare brown land and rocky hills rise from the water, streaming and glistening. Radiant golden light breaks over the new coastlines, and the gathered seas shine between the emerging continents under a pale, clean sky full of promise.

In warm midday sunshine, seen from a low hillside, a wide rolling valley bursts into green: grass sweeps across the hills like a wave, flowering herbs open, and young fruit trees rise heavy with figs, pomegranates and olives. The fresh land glistens beneath a radiant sky, still empty of any creature, quiet and new.

At twilight, seen from a high mountain ridge above a green land and a calm sea, a blazing golden sun sinks on one horizon while a great silver moon rises on the other. The first stars kindle across the deepening blue sky, and the new lights of heaven shine in radiant order, marking days, seasons and years.

On a bright, breezy morning, seen from just above the sparkling waves, great whales breach and spout, dolphins leap, and shoals of fish flash beneath the surface near a rocky coast. Flocks of birds of every kind wheel across a radiant sky, gulls, herons and eagles, the waters and the air suddenly teeming with joyful life.

On a golden afternoon, seen from above, a broad grassland comes alive: lions, elephants, horses, deer and camels roam across the plain, cattle graze beside a winding river, and small creatures scurry through the grass. A soft radiance lies over the whole land, and every animal moves in peace beneath a warm, hazy sky.

In a lush riverside meadow at early morning, seen at ground level, a column of radiant light falls from the parting clouds onto Adam and Eve, newly made, standing together among tall flowering reeds and ferns that screen their bodies, Eve's long hair falling around her. Animals and birds gather at a distance, and the couple look up in wonder at the blessing.

At sunset on the sixth day, seen from a gentle hill, Adam and Eve stand among fruit-laden trees and tall flowering plants that screen them, gazing over a vast garden where lions, lambs, deer and birds feed side by side on green herbs. Warm, radiant golden light floods the whole creation, and everything glows with calm, perfect goodness.

Seen from high above on a calm, cloudless afternoon, the finished world lies at rest: a light haze hangs over quiet lakes and forests, rivers wind through green valleys, and herds lie sleeping in the meadows. A soft radiant glow rests over the whole earth, and nothing stirs in the deep, holy stillness of the seventh day.

Before sunrise on a bare reddish plain where no plant yet grows, seen from a low hill, a soft mist rises from the ground and drifts over the dry earth. In the middle of the plain, in a shaft of radiant light from the sky, Adam lies on the red earth he was formed from, veiled by swirling mist, drawing his first breath as he begins to rise.

On a bright morning, seen at ground level, the garden of Eden spreads across a green valley full of fruit trees, flowering shrubs and sparkling streams under a radiant sky. At its centre stand two great trees, the tree of life glowing softly and the tree of knowledge heavy with fruit, while Adam walks among tall ferns that screen him, gazing around in delight.

From high in the sky at hazy midday, a shining river flows out of the green garden of Eden and divides into four great rivers that wind away in different directions, across golden desert, rolling hills and dark forest. Along one riverbank, nuggets of gold and pale gemstones glint in the sand, and the whole land feels vast and abundant.

On a warm, misty morning in the heart of the garden, seen from across a small clearing, Adam stands among tall ferns and flowering plants before the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, its branches heavy with gleaming fruit. A beam of radiant light falls between him and the tree as he listens to the solemn command, the garden peaceful all around.

In a golden late-afternoon meadow beside a river, seen from a hillside, Adam stands on a low rise among tall grasses that screen him, raising his hand as lions, horses, deer, camels and oxen file past in pairs and birds swoop overhead. A soft radiance lies over the scene; every creature has its mate, yet Adam stands alone.

In a quiet, dew-covered glade at early morning, seen at ground level, Adam rises from sleep beneath a great tree as Eve is led toward him in a soft radiant glow. Both are screened by tall flowering plants and Eve's long hair; Adam reaches out in joyful wonder, and the two meet in innocent happiness while birds sing in the branches.

In the middle of the garden on a warm, still afternoon, seen from slightly above, Eve stands among tall ferns and lilies, her long hair falling around her, beside the tree of knowledge heavy with gleaming fruit. A large, beautiful serpent coils along a low branch with its head close to her, speaking smoothly, and she listens with curiosity in the dappled, faintly uneasy light.

Beneath the tree of knowledge in late afternoon, seen at ground level, Eve holds out a bitten fruit to Adam, who takes it, both screened by dense fig trees and tall plants. A cloud's shadow passes over the garden, the light turns grey, and they look at each other in sudden shame, pulling broad fig leaves from the branches to make aprons.

In the cool of the evening, seen from above through the branches, a breeze stirs the garden and long golden light slants between the trees as a radiant glow moves along a path among them. Adam and Eve, in rough fig-leaf aprons, crouch fearfully behind thick bushes and tall ferns; Adam points toward Eve, and the serpent slips away through the grass.

Under dark, gathering storm clouds, seen from a rise, a beam of stern radiant light falls on the garden as the serpent slithers away on its belly into the dust. Adam and Eve stand with heads bowed among tall plants in their fig-leaf aprons, and beyond the garden's edge the ground turns to thorns and thistles stretching toward a barren, wind-swept land.

At a soft, misty dawn in a clearing of the garden, seen at ground level, Adam and Eve stand wrapped in long garments of skins, touching the warm fur in quiet wonder, bathed in a gentle beam of radiant light. Adam turns to Eve, naming her the mother of all living, and their sorrow is mixed with tender comfort.

At dusk, seen from above the eastern gate of Eden, Adam and Eve in their garments of skins walk away into a bare, rocky land, heads bowed, glancing back. Behind them mighty Cherubim, glowing with radiant light, stand at the garden's entrance beside a flaming sword that turns every way, its fire lighting the darkening sky and the lush garden they have lost.

At bright spring midday in a wide valley east of Eden, seen from a hillside, Cain breaks the dark soil with a wooden hoe beside rows of young grain, while Abel leads a flock of sheep across the green slopes beyond. Adam and Eve, in garments of skins, watch their two grown sons from beside a simple hut of branches and stone.

On a hilltop in the early morning, seen from the slope below, two stone altars stand side by side. Smoke from Abel's altar rises straight up into a radiant beam of light from the clouds as he kneels with his flock behind him, while smoke from Cain's altar of grain and fruit drifts low and dark, and Cain stands apart in its shadow, fists clenched, angry and downcast.

On a hot, hazy afternoon, seen from a low rise behind them, Cain and Abel walk out together into a wide, empty field of tall golden grain, Abel talking easily while Cain walks tense and silent. Their shadows stretch beside them, a line of dark storm clouds builds over the distant hills, and an ominous stillness hangs over the land.

At dusk under a heavy, bruised-purple sky, seen from above, Cain stands alone in the middle of a wide, darkening field, shoulders hunched and one hand raised defensively, as a beam of stern radiant light falls on him from the clouds. Far off, Abel's sheep wander untended on the hillside, and the field lies silent and accusing.

In the cold grey light before dawn, seen from a distance, Cain walks away eastward across barren, stony hills toward the desolate land of Nod, carrying a bundle and a staff, a faint glow resting on his brow. He looks back over his shoulder at a distant shaft of radiant light above the green land he is leaving, a lonely fugitive in a vast, empty landscape.

Seen from above in the late morning, the first city rises in the land of Nod, low mud-brick walls and houses beside a river, with Cain watching from its gate. Outside the walls his descendants thrive: herdsmen with tents and cattle, a musician playing a harp and pipe, and a smith hammering bronze at a glowing forge.

At night by a roaring campfire outside a cluster of tents, seen at ground level, Lamech, a fierce bearded man in a heavy cloak, stands with his arm raised, boasting to his two wives, Adah and Zillah, who sit by the fire looking up at him uneasily. Firelight flickers on the tent walls, and darkness presses in all around.

At sunrise on a green hillside, seen from a little below, Adam and Eve hold their newborn son Seth beside a simple stone altar, where their growing household gathers with hands raised to call upon the LORD. Soft golden light spreads across the valley, and the scene is full of quiet hope after long grief.

On a warm late afternoon in a broad valley dotted with tents and dwellings, seen at ground level, Adam sits on a stone seat at the end of his long life, surrounded by a great family of sons, daughters and grandchildren, with his grown son Seth at his side. Fields and flocks stretch into the hazy distance, and the low sun casts long, gentle shadows.

Seen from a high hillside at midday, a great clan of many generations spreads through a fertile valley: white-bearded patriarchs lead grown sons and daughters, children run among the flocks, and new tents and fields reach toward the distant hills. A caravan of families with donkeys follows the river, life multiplying across the land.

At misty dawn, seen from the valley below, Enoch, an old man with a staff, walks steadily up a mountain path into a brilliant column of radiant light pouring down from the clouds, his figure fading into the glow. In the foreground his family stands among their tents, looking up in awe and wonder as he disappears.

At golden evening on hard, stony farmland, seen from a little above, a family gathers outside their tents: the aged Methuselah leans on a staff, his son Lamech rests from his toil, and Noah stands with Noah's sons beside him, looking out over the weary fields. Tired oxen and wooden ploughs rest nearby, and the warm light holds a hope of comfort.

At noon, seen from above the gate of a sprawling early city, people throng the streets as a lavish wedding procession passes with music and garlands, while towering warriors of enormous stature, the mighty men of renown, stride through the crowd with spears. Above, dark clouds gather over the city, pierced by a single stern beam of radiant light.

Seen from high above at night, a sprawling city of the ancient world is full of violence: torch-lit streets of brawling crowds, a house in flames, people fleeing through the shadows. Heavy storm clouds roll in over it, and a dim, sorrowful light glows behind them, as if heaven itself grieves over the earth.

In clear morning light, seen from a hillside, Noah walks with Noah's wife and Noah's sons along a quiet path through green fields far from the city, a soft beam of radiant light resting on the little family. Behind them on the horizon, smoke rises over the corrupt city, and the rest of the land lies dark under brooding clouds.

In a forest clearing of tall cypress-like gopher-wood trees in the late afternoon, Noah stands looking up into a radiant beam of light that pierces the canopy, listening intently, one hand on a great trunk. Shafts of light fall through the forest, and through a gap in the trees a dark, storm-heavy horizon hints at the coming flood.

Seen from above on a wide dry plain under a hot midday sun, the immense wooden hull of the ark rises on scaffolding, three stories high. Noah directs the work as Noah's sons haul timbers and brush black pitch from steaming pots, while Noah's wife and the sons' wives carry baskets of grain into the storerooms, a soft radiant light resting on the great ship.

At calm evening, seen at ground level across the grass, the finished ark stands enormous on a dry plain, its great door open in its side with a ramp leading up. Noah stands small at the foot of the ramp, looking up into a beam of radiant light breaking from the clouds, while the first pairs of animals and birds gather around the ship.

Seen from above under a heavy grey sky, long lines of animals walk two and two up the ramp into the ark: elephants, lions, giraffes, sheep and camels, with birds circling overhead. Noah, Noah's wife and Noah's sons stand at the great door guiding them in, the sons' wives beside them, as the wind rises across the empty plain.

At ground level in a sudden, violent storm, torrents of rain pour from a black sky and fountains of water burst from the cracking earth around the ark. The last pairs of animals hurry up the ramp, and as Noah, Noah's wife and Noah's sons look out from the doorway, a radiant glow surrounds the great door as it swings shut.

In driving rain, seen from just above the waves, the ark floats high on a vast, heaving grey sea, lifted far above the vanished land. Only the last rocky mountain peaks still break the surface in the distance, wrapped in swirling cloud, and the waters keep rising beneath a dark, endless sky.

Seen from high above, the lone ark drifts on a boundless, calm ocean that stretches to every horizon, with no land, tree or living creature anywhere in sight. The rain has thinned, a pale silver light filters through a low, unbroken overcast, and the tiny ship floats on in vast, desolate silence.

At a windy dawn, seen from a neighbouring slope, a strong wind sweeps the clouds apart and radiant golden sunbeams pour down as the floodwaters slowly recede. The great ark rests on a high ridge of the mountains of Ararat, and around it rocky peaks emerge one by one from the shining water, bringing a feeling of fresh hope.

On a grey, misty midday, seen from below the ark's high side, Noah leans out of the opened window as the ship rests on the mountain, releasing a white dove into the air while a black raven flies to and fro over the endless waters. Mist hangs over half-submerged peaks, and Noah watches with patient hope.

At golden sunset, seen from across the water, a white dove flies back toward the ark with a fresh olive leaf in its beak, glowing in the low light. Noah reaches out from the high window with open hands, Noah's wife and Noah's sons crowd behind him in joy, and below, the receding waters reveal green hillsides and treetops.

On a cool, clear morning, seen from above, Noah, Noah's wife and Noah's sons stand on the roof of the ark where its covering has been pulled back, high on the mountains of Ararat. Below them the land stretches dry and green to the horizon, streams glinting in the valleys, and they gaze in quiet amazement at the renewed earth.

At warm midday under drifting white clouds, seen from a slope below, animals of every kind pour out of the ark's open door and stream down the green mountainside: horses gallop, deer bound, and birds burst into the sky. Noah, Noah's wife and Noah's sons walk down the ramp behind them in a soft beam of radiant light, full of joy.

In the golden evening on a mountain shelf below the ark, seen from a little above, Noah kneels before a newly built stone altar, smoke from his offering rising straight up into a radiant beam of light. Noah's wife and Noah's sons kneel behind him, and green valleys stretch away toward the horizon, where fields await seedtime and harvest.

On a fresh, breezy morning, seen from the valley below, Noah and Noah's sons stand on a grassy hillside beneath a beam of radiant light, with Noah's wife and the sons' wives beside them, raising their hands to receive the blessing. Around them the wide valleys lie open and empty, and herds of deer and wild beasts keep a wary distance.

In the late afternoon after a passing rain, seen from behind the family, a brilliant rainbow arches across a dark cloud over a broad green valley, glowing with radiant light. Noah, Noah's wife and Noah's sons stand on the wet grass with animals and birds all around them, looking up in wonder at the sign of the everlasting covenant.

On a bright late-summer morning, seen from across the valley, terraced hillsides are covered with rows of heavy grapevines. Noah carries a basket of grapes among the vines while Noah's sons and their families harvest and tread grapes in a stone winepress; beside the vineyard stands Noah's dark goat-hair tent, its flap closed, with wine jars stacked by the door.

At dusk outside Noah's goat-hair tent, faintly lit from within by an oil lamp, two of Noah's sons walk backward toward the doorway with a cloak spread across their shoulders between them, their faces turned away. Their brother Ham, who has just told them, stands a short way off, and the vineyard lies quiet in the fading light.

Under a pale overcast morning sky, seen from a little above, Noah stands outside his tent among the vineyards with one arm raised, pronouncing words over his sons. Two of Noah's sons kneel before him to receive his blessing, while Ham stands apart with his young son Canaan, head lowered, and the quiet hills stretch away behind them.

From a high coastal headland at sunrise, Noah's sons watch as their descendants spread across the earth: on the shore below, Japheth's people load small wooden boats and sail out across a glittering sea toward distant green islands and coastlands. Families, flocks and bundles crowd the beach, and the wide world opens before them.

Under a hot midday sun on the wide plain of Shinar, seen at ground level, Nimrod, a powerful hunter with a great bow and a leopard-skin cloak, strides ahead of his followers and hounds through tall grass. Behind him along the river, crowds of workers raise the mud-brick walls and towers of new cities, the beginning of his kingdom.

On a cool, cloudy day with patches of sun, seen from a hillside, a long caravan of Canaanite clans with donkeys, flocks and tents winds down through green, rolling hills toward the sea, where a small harbour town sits on the coast. Family after family settles along the way, pitching tents in the valleys, while a fertile plain shimmers far to the south.

At sunset, seen from high above a wide plateau, long caravans of Shem's descendants travel eastward toward a distant mountain range, their camels and donkeys laden with tents. At a fork in the road the clans divide, some turning one way and some another, families waving farewell as the earth seems to part beneath a vast orange sky.

On the flat plain of Shinar on a hot, bright morning, seen from above, crowds of people who share one language work together: they mould mud bricks in long rows, fire them in smoking kilns and carry them up ramps to the broad base of a great tower rising beside a new city. Pots of bitumen bubble, and everyone works with proud, confident energy.

At dusk, seen from far across the plain, the enormous half-built tower of Babel rises in stepped tiers toward the clouds, its scaffolding swarming with tiny workers. A radiant column of light descends from the parting clouds onto the plain beside the tower, and the builders pause and look up, small and uncertain beneath the glow.

Under a windy, storm-grey sky, seen from high above, the unfinished tower of Babel stands abandoned, ropes and ladders dangling from its broken top. Across the plain, crowds stream away in every direction, families gesturing at one another in confusion, unable to understand each other's speech, while a stern shaft of radiant light falls on the deserted city.

On a clear morning in green highland pastures, seen from a hillside, a caravan of generations moves down a river valley: white-bearded patriarchs lead the way on donkeys, followed by their sons, daughters and grandchildren with flocks of sheep and goats. Tents are pitched on the slopes behind them, and the long family line stretches far back into the hills.

In the golden afternoon along the broad Euphrates, seen at ground level, Shem's descendants settle in farming villages among date palms and canals, the brick towers of Ur rising in the distance. In front, the patriarch Terah stands with his three grown sons, Abraham, Nahor and Haran, looking out over the flat, fertile land as their families work the fields.

At dusk, seen from a rooftop above a mud-brick courtyard in Ur, with the great stepped temple tower dark against an orange sky, Terah's family mourns the death of Haran. Old Terah sits grieving while Abraham and Sarah stand with the fatherless Lot and with Nahor and Milcah; Sarah, who has no child, gazes wistfully at children playing in the lane.

At dawn, seen from a distance along the riverbank, a small caravan of camels and donkeys leaves the walls of Ur and winds northwest beside the Euphrates, the city's temple tower fading in the haze behind them. Old Terah rides in front, with Abraham, Sarah and Lot walking beside the laden animals, setting out on the long road toward Haran and Canaan.

At dawn on the wide plain outside the mud-brick town of Haran, Abraham stands alone among his grazing flocks, lifting his face toward a brilliant beam of light that breaks through the clouds and falls around him. The town's walls and flat roofs lie behind him in soft blue shadow, and he listens, still and awed.

Seen from high above on a clear morning, a long caravan winds west out of Haran across golden grassland: Abraham walks at its head with his staff, Sarah rides a camel beside him and Lot follows close behind, with servants, laden donkeys, folded tents and great flocks of sheep and goats stretching back toward the distant town.

In the green plain of Moreh at Shechem, between two rounded mountains, Abraham sets the last stone on a simple altar beside a great spreading oak as a column of golden light descends from the afternoon sky onto the place. Sarah and Lot watch in wonder from the tents, and a Canaanite village clings to the far hillside.

Seen from a neighbouring hillside at sunset, Abraham's dark goat-hair tents stand in a row along a high ridge, and thin smoke rises from a stone altar where he stands with his arms raised, calling on the LORD. Far to the west the small walled town of Bethel glows orange in the last light, while Ai sits in blue shadow to the east.

Under a hard white midday sun, the weary caravan halts on a cracked, famine-parched ridge where the desert ends, and below spreads the green Nile valley with its palm groves, fields and distant temples. Beside a kneeling camel, Abraham speaks urgently to Sarah, gesturing toward Egypt, and she listens, troubled and uneasy.

In the cool morning light of Pharaoh's palace courtyard beside the Nile, Egyptians of the royal court lead Sarah up broad stone steps between tall columns toward Pharaoh, who waits on a shaded terrace above. Below, surrounded by Pharaoh's gifts of sheep, oxen, donkeys, camels and servants, Abraham stands helpless, watching her go.

At dusk, dark storm clouds churn over Pharaoh's palace, lit from within by a strange, fierce glow, and stricken servants lie sick on mats along the colonnade. At the great gate, Pharaoh points angrily toward the desert as he gives Sarah back to Abraham, and Egyptian soldiers escort their caravan of flocks, camels and servants out of the land.

On a fresh spring morning, a rich caravan climbs back into the green hill country: herds of cattle, camels laden with chests of silver and gold, servants and flocks. On the ridge between Bethel and Ai, Abraham kneels in prayer at his old, weathered stone altar, while Sarah and Lot lead the long line up the slope behind him.

At a crowded stone well on a dusty, overgrazed hillside in the midday heat, the herdsmen of Abraham and the herdsmen of Lot shout and shove each other with raised staffs while their sheep and cattle jostle for water. The grass is eaten bare, and Abraham and Lot hurry down toward the quarrel from their two great camps of tents crowded on the slopes above.

Seen from behind and above on a high hilltop in golden late-afternoon light, Abraham sweeps his arm across the land as he speaks peaceably to Lot. Lot gazes east, down to the plain of Jordan, lush and well watered like a garden, its river glinting and its distant cities shimmering in the haze.

From high above at dusk, Lot's long line of herds, servants and tents winds down from the hills into the green plain of Jordan toward the walled city of Sodom, over which a dark, sullen haze hangs. Behind on the hilltop, Abraham stands small beside his tents, watching them go.

column4: All the land which thou seest
column7: Alone on the highest hilltop under a vast, clear morning sky, Abraham turns to look north, south, east and west over endless folded hills and valleys, as radiant light streams down around him and the wind lifts the dust at his feet. Far to the south, the great oaks of Mamre, where he will pitch his tent and build an altar, catch the sun.

At dawn beside a broad river in the east, four kings in rich robes and tall headdresses confer before a great stepped temple tower, while their vast army camp of tents, spears and pack donkeys spreads across the plain behind them, making ready to march west against the five rebel kings of the cities of the plain.

Seen from a high ridge, Chedorlaomer's huge army snakes through the red sandstone mountains of Seir under a blazing midday sun, spears glinting and dust boiling up behind it. On distant hilltops, smoke drifts up from conquered strongholds, and frightened herdsmen drive their flocks away into the wilderness.

column4: Battle in the vale of Siddim
column7: In the hazy vale of Siddim beside the Salt Sea, two armies clash in clouds of dust under a copper-coloured afternoon sky. The kings of Sodom and Gomorrah flee in panic with their guards, stumbling among black, bubbling tar pits, while the rest of their soldiers scatter up the slopes of the bare brown mountains.

Seen from a hillside at evening, the victorious eastern army marches away from plundered Sodom in a long column heading north, its donkeys piled high with grain sacks, jars and bundles of goods. Among the roped captives trudging in the dust walks Lot with his head bowed, his wife and daughters close behind him.

Under the great oaks of Mamre in the early morning, a dust-covered man who has escaped the battle kneels breathless before Abraham, pointing north. Around them the camp springs into motion as Abraham's three hundred and eighteen trained servants take up spears, bows and shields and form ranks among the tents, and his Amorite allies arrive to join them.

At night in the hills near Damascus, Abraham's men sweep into the enemy camp from several sides with blazing torches, and the startled raiders flee into the darkness, leaving tents and plunder behind. By a campfire, Abraham helps Lot to his feet and cuts his bonds, as freed women and captives gather around in relief.

In the broad king's dale below the hill town of Salem, under a soft golden morning sky, Melchizedek steps forward with bread and a cup of wine and lifts his hand to bless Abraham, who bows before him and gives him a tenth of all. Behind them wait the men with the recovered flocks and goods, as the king of Sodom approaches with his attendants.

column4: Not a thread nor a shoelatchet
column7: At ground level in the same valley under high, thin midday clouds, the king of Sodom, in rich embroidered robes, gestures eagerly toward heaped spoils of gold vessels, fine cloth and jars. Abraham stands firm with one hand raised toward heaven, refusing to take even a thread, while his allies Aner, Eshcol and Mamre and their men rest and eat beside the recovered flocks.

At dusk beside the oaks of Mamre, Abraham sits alone at the door of his tent, troubled and childless, as a radiant light glows within the evening clouds above him. Across the quiet camp, his steward Eliezer of Damascus, a grey-bearded man with a staff, directs servants carrying water jars between the tents by lamplight.

Late at night on the open hillside outside the camp, Abraham stands with his arms lifted beneath a breathtaking sky crowded with countless stars and the bright band of the Milky Way. A soft heavenly light surrounds him on the dark grass, and the tents below glow faintly, as he gazes upward in wonder and believes.

On a sunlit hillside in the afternoon, Abraham has laid out the offering of a heifer, a goat and a ram in two facing rows on flat stones, with a turtledove and a young pigeon at the end and a path left between. Vultures swoop down, and Abraham drives them off with his staff, while light shines from a bright cloud above.

As the red sun sinks behind the hills, Abraham lies in a deep sleep on the ground beside the rows of the offering, and a great, dreadful darkness rolls down over him like a thick cloud, swallowing the sunset. Within the darkness glows a faint, solemn light, and the empty land around lies hushed and still.

Seen from above in the full darkness of night, a smoking clay furnace and a blazing torch pass slowly along the path between the two rows of the offering, lighting the hillside in flickering orange. Abraham kneels nearby in awe, while beyond him the vast promised land stretches away under the stars toward faint, distant rivers.

In the camp at Mamre on a still, overcast morning, Sarah leads her Egyptian maid Hagar by the hand across the open ground toward Abraham, who rises from his seat at the tent door. Hagar walks with lowered eyes, Sarah is sad but resolved, and a few servant women watch quietly from the shade of the oaks.

In the hot, glaring afternoon, Sarah stands at the tent door angrily confronting Abraham, who spreads his hands and turns away from the quarrel. Beyond the last tents, Hagar, a hand on her belly and a small bundle on her shoulder, hurries alone into the bare, shimmering wilderness, glancing back at the camp.

At first light in the vast, stony wilderness on the road to Shur, a small spring bubbles up among a few palms and reeds. Hagar kneels beside the water with her hands lifted in wonder as an angel stands before her, speaking of the son she will bear, and a gentle radiance spreads from the sky over the lonely place.

At golden evening in the camp at Mamre, Abraham stands outside the tents joyfully lifting his newborn son, wrapped in cloth, toward the sky as he names him. Hagar rests on cushions in the tent doorway, servants gather smiling with lamps, and Sarah watches quietly from the door of her own tent apart.

In the bright morning at Mamre, Abraham lies face down on the ground in front of his tents as a dazzling pillar of light descends from the sky before him, making the great oaks glow. At a distance his servants and flocks stand still, shielding their eyes, sensing something holy as God speaks his everlasting covenant.

From high above at midday, Abraham stands on a rise at the edge of his great encampment, bathed in radiant light from the sky, listening intently. Below him spreads his whole household: rows of tents, herdsmen with flocks, men carrying water and boys at play, Ishmael among them, all the men and boys who will share the covenant.

Seen from across the camp in the hazy heat of early afternoon, Abraham kneels with his face bowed to the ground, shaking with astonished laughter at the promise of a son from Sarah, as soft light pours from a bright cloud above him. Nearby, Sarah sits spinning wool at her tent door, unaware, and Ishmael practises with his bow under the oaks.

In the late afternoon, under towering white clouds edged with gold, the column of radiant light lifts slowly from the ground before Abraham and rises into the sky as God goes up from him. Abraham stands alone among the oaks of Mamre with his face turned upward, holding the promise of a son, while his camp waits quietly behind him.

At dusk on the same day, all the men and boys of Abraham's household, those born in his tents and those bought from strangers, stand gathered in a great, solemn crowd before his tent under the oaks. Abraham stands at the front with his hand on Ishmael's shoulder, and evening fires glow quietly across the camp.

In the shimmering heat of midday at Mamre, three Angels stand quietly near a great spreading oak, and a gentle radiance rests over the place. Abraham, who has run from the shade of his tent door, bows to the ground before them, begging them to stay, rest under the tree and wash their dusty feet.

Seen from a little above, the camp bustles in the afternoon heat: Sarah kneels at a smoking hearth by the tent, baking flat cakes, a young servant hurries from the herd leading a calf, and Abraham stands attentively under the oak beside the three Angels, who sit eating bread, butter, milk and meat on a spread cloth.

At ground level in the long golden light of late afternoon, the three Angels sit under the oak with Abraham standing before them, a soft radiance over the gathering, as one of them promises a son. Behind Abraham, Sarah stands half hidden in the tent doorway with her hand over her mouth, laughing to herself, then shrinking back afraid.

Seen from behind on a high, rocky ridge east of Mamre in the early evening, Abraham walks with the three Angels, seeing them on their way. They stop at the edge and look down over the vast plain of Jordan, where the distant cities of Sodom and Gomorrah lie under a dark, brooding haze, while a beam of light breaks from the clouds above.

At sunset on the ridge, two of the Angels walk away down the long path toward the plain and Sodom, small figures in the reddening light. Abraham stays behind, standing alone before a column of radiant light, stepping forward with his hands spread wide, boldly pleading for the righteous of the city below.

In the deep blue twilight, with the first stars appearing, Abraham kneels humbly in the dust of the ridge with open hands, still pleading, now for only ten righteous. The radiant light before him begins to rise and fade into the sky, and far below, the cities of the plain sit dark and silent beside the gleaming Salt Sea.

In the last orange light of evening at the massive stone gateway of Sodom, Lot rises from his seat among the elders and bows low with his face toward the ground before two Angels who have just arrived from the road. Behind them the city's crowded streets glow with lamplight, and sullen faces watch from the shadows.

Seen from the rooftops at night, an angry mob of the men of Sodom, young and old, fills the narrow torch-lit street around Lot's house, shouting and pressing forward. Lot stands alone before his shut door with his hands raised, pleading with them, as the crowd surges closer to break it down.

In the same dark street at ground level, Lot's door swings open in a burst of brilliant white light as the two Angels pull him inside to safety. Outside, the mob reels back dazzled and blinded, men stumbling, groping along the walls and dropping their torches, unable to find the door.

Late at night under a thin moon, Lot hurries through Sodom's dark, empty lanes to a lamplit doorway, where his two sons-in-law, young men in fine robes, lean laughing and wave him away as if he were joking, while he points urgently toward the sky and the city gate.

In the grey half-light before sunrise, the two Angels hurry Lot, his wife and his two daughters through the great gate of Sodom, holding them firmly by the hands as Lot lingers and looks back. The sleeping city lies behind them under a heavy, ominous sky, and the open plain stretches ahead.

Seen from high above as the eastern sky turns pink, one of the Angels points urgently toward the distant mountains, while Lot pleads and points instead to the little walled town of Zoar nearby on the plain. His wife and daughters clutch their bundles on the road, and a strange, heavy stillness hangs over the green fields and the city behind.

As the sun rises, fire and burning brimstone pour from a blazing sky onto Sodom and Gomorrah, engulfing the distant walls and towers in flame and smoke. Near the gate of little Zoar, Lot and his two daughters run for shelter, while behind them on the road stands a white pillar of salt in the shape of a woman looking back.

Early in the morning, Abraham stands alone on the high ridge where he pleaded the day before, leaning on his staff. Far below, the whole plain is gone: enormous columns of black smoke rise from the land as from a furnace, darkening the morning sky, while he looks on in silent grief.

High in the barren, rocky mountains above the ruined plain, a lonely cave glows with firelight on a cold, windy night. Lot sits hunched and weary by the small fire inside the entrance, while his two daughters stand together at the cliff's edge, whispering, looking out over the dark, empty, smoking land where no one is left.

On a clear morning in the high, rugged mountains east of the Salt Sea, Lot's two daughters sit outside the cave mouth, each cradling a newborn son, while Lot sits nearby in silence. Beyond them, empty brown hills and plateaus roll away to the east, the lands their sons' peoples, Moab and Ammon, will one day fill.

In the dry south country near the walled town of Gerar, under a hazy afternoon sky, servants of King Abimelech escort Sarah away from Abraham's tents toward the town gate. Abraham, who has called her his sister, stands among his flocks watching in silence, while Sarah walks with quiet dignity between the king's men.

On the flat palace roof of Gerar under a starry night sky, King Abimelech, a bearded man in a linen night robe, starts up from his sleeping couch in terror as a radiant light pours down upon him from the heavens. All around, the sleeping town and its dark walls spread out in moonlit silence.

Early in the morning in the palace courtyard of Gerar, Abimelech's servants huddle together in fear along the walls. On a raised seat in the shade, Abimelech leans forward and points accusingly at Abraham, who stands before him with open hands, explaining that he feared for his life because of his wife.

Outside the gates of Gerar in bright midday sun, Abimelech returns Sarah to Abraham's side and sweeps his arm over the open land before them, offering him any place to dwell. His servants lead out sheep, oxen, menservants and maidservants as gifts and set down a heavy chest of a thousand pieces of silver at Abraham's feet.

In the soft rose light of evening, Abraham stands before the palace of Gerar with his arms lifted to heaven in prayer. A warm radiance falls from the clouds over the royal house, and Abimelech, his queen and the women of his household come out onto the steps, healed and wondering.

In golden morning light at Abraham's camp, Sarah sits at the door of her tent cradling her newborn son and laughing with joy, as Abraham stands beside her with his hands lifted in thanks. Servant women and herdsmen crowd around, laughing with her, and a warm radiance falls from the sky over the tents.

At a great feast among the tents in the afternoon, guests sit on rugs before platters of food beneath striped awnings, celebrating little Isaac, a small child of about three, who stands beside his mother. Nearby Ishmael mocks and laughs, and Sarah turns to Abraham, pointing at Hagar and her son, while Abraham stands stricken with grief.

At pale dawn at the edge of the camp, Abraham lays a skin of water and a bundle of bread on Hagar's shoulder, heavy with sorrow, as Ishmael stands beside her. A quiet beam of light breaks through the morning clouds above them, and ahead the empty wilderness of Beer-sheba stretches away into the haze.

Seen from high above at scorching midday, the bare, cracked wilderness of Beer-sheba stretches in every direction. Ishmael lies weak in the thin shade of a small desert shrub, and a bowshot away Hagar sits alone on the hot ground with her face in her hands, weeping, the empty water skin lying limp beside her.

In the late afternoon, a radiant beam breaks through the sky over the wilderness, and an angel calls to Hagar from within the light. Filled with hope, Hagar kneels at a stone well she had not seen before, filling the water skin, while Ishmael sits up beside her and drinks gratefully, the desert glowing gold around them.

Years later, in the rugged red wilderness of Paran at sunrise, Ishmael, now a grown man, stands on a rocky outcrop drawing his bow toward a distant herd of gazelles. Below, Hagar welcomes a young Egyptian bride arriving on a camel at their small cluster of tents beside a spring, the desert alive with morning light.

At a stone well on the open plain of Beer-sheba in late morning, King Abimelech and Phichol, the armoured captain of his host, stand with a few soldiers before Abraham under a windy, cloud-dappled sky. Abraham agrees to swear peace, then points firmly at the well his own herdsmen dug, which the king's servants had seized.

In warm afternoon light at the well of Beer-sheba, Abraham's servants drive sheep and oxen over to Abimelech's men as a covenant gift. Seven white ewe lambs stand apart by themselves beside the well, and Abimelech gestures toward them, curious, as he and Abraham clasp hands and swear their oath of peace.

At sunset at Beer-sheba, Abraham kneels to plant a young tamarisk tree beside the well among a new grove of saplings, then lifts his face to call on the everlasting God. His tents and flocks rest peacefully on the plain, and the hills of the Philistines' land glow purple in the west.

Deep in a still night at Beer-sheba, Abraham steps out of his tent among the dark tamarisk trees as a radiant light shines down upon him from the sky. He stands frozen, a hand pressed to his chest in anguish, while behind him a lamp glows softly through the door of the tent where his beloved son sleeps.

On the misty third morning, the little party crests a ridge in rugged, rocky hill country: two young servants, a saddled donkey loaded with split firewood, Abraham and Isaac (boy). Abraham lifts his eyes and points toward a lone mountain far off in the blue haze, telling the young men to wait there with the donkey.

On a steep, stony path winding up the bare mountain under a bright, cloudless late-morning sky, Isaac (boy) climbs with the bundle of wood tied on his back and looks up to ask his father where the lamb is. Beside him, Abraham carries a small clay pot of fire and answers gently, and the two walk on together.

At noon on the windswept summit of Moriah, Isaac (boy) lies quietly on the wood atop the rough stone altar Abraham has built. Abraham stands over him, then suddenly halts and looks up as an angel appears in a blaze of light breaking through the clouds, calling his name and stopping his hand.

Moments later on the mountaintop, Abraham turns and finds a ram caught by its curling horns in a thorny thicket behind him, and wrestles it free with joy. Isaac (boy), unbound, sits up on the edge of the altar watching in relief, while the wide hills of Moriah spread out below in the clear afternoon light.

As evening falls, Abraham and Isaac (boy) stand side by side on the summit beside the altar's thin rising smoke, bathed in radiant light pouring from the heavens as the promise is spoken. The first stars appear in the deepening sky, and far below, the two young servants wait with the donkey for the road home to Beer-sheba.

Far to the north in the green country of Haran, the large family of Nahor gathers among its tents and mud-brick houses in mellow morning sun: white-bearded Nahor, his wife Milcah with her eight grown sons and their households, his second wife Reumah with her four children, and Bethuel cradling his infant daughter.

At dusk among the oak-dotted hills of Hebron, Abraham kneels weeping in the dust before a large goat-hair tent, its door open on the lamplit place where his wife's body lies shrouded in white linen on a low bier. Servants and women of the household sit nearby with covered heads in silent grief as the grey evening settles over the camp.

column4: Abraham asks for a burial place
column7: In the broad stone gateway of Hebron on a clear morning, Abraham, still in mourning, bows low before the Hittite elders, bearded men in striped robes seated on stone benches along the wall, who answer him with respect. Townspeople crowd the square to listen, and beyond the gate a green field with a dark cave at its far end lies among the trees.

Seen from a rooftop above Hebron's crowded gate at midday, Ephron the Hittite, a richly robed landowner, gestures toward his field while Abraham weighs out four hundred shekels of silver on a bronze balance set on a cloth, the bright pieces heaped in its pan. Elders and passers-by gather round as witnesses under a hot blue sky.

Seen from a hillside in the late afternoon, a quiet procession winds across Ephron's field before Mamre, ringed with old trees, toward the dark mouth of the cave of Machpelah in a rocky slope. Abraham walks at its head in grief as servants carry his wife's body, wrapped in white linen, on a bier, and the household follows with bowed heads in soft golden light.

Under a great oak beside his tents on a clear morning, the aged Abraham sits on a cushioned seat as Abraham's servant kneels before him, one hand beneath his master's thigh near the knee in the ancient gesture of an oath, solemnly swearing to seek a wife for his son among his kin. Camels, flocks and herdsmen fill the sunlit camp around them, signs of how richly Abraham has been blessed.

Seen from a low rise in the late afternoon, ten laden camels kneel beside a stone well outside the walled city of Nahor, and Abraham's servant stands among them with hands lifted in prayer, asking for a sign. Women in long robes stream out of the city gate with clay pitchers on their shoulders, and the low sun turns the dusty plain and mud-brick walls amber.

At the stone well in the golden light of sunset, Rebekah tips her clay pitcher into a long stone trough where ten thirsty camels jostle to drink, ready to hurry back down the well steps for more. Abraham's servant stands a little apart, leaning on his staff and watching her in silent wonder, as the walls of Nahor glow behind them.

In the deep blue twilight by the well, with the camels resting and the first stars appearing, Rebekah stands amazed, wearing the gold nose ring and heavy gold bracelets the stranger has just given her. Before her, Abraham's servant bows his head to the ground in worship, overcome with thankfulness, while lamps begin to glow along the walls of Nahor behind them.

Seen from the flat rooftop, torches light the courtyard of Bethuel's house as Laban strides forward with open arms to welcome Abraham's servant as one blessed of the LORD. Household servants unsaddle the ten camels, spread straw and pour water over the travellers' dusty feet, while Rebekah watches from a doorway, her gold bracelets catching the firelight.

The wide main room of Bethuel's house glows with oil lamps at night, and a low table is spread with bread, roasted meat and fruit, but Abraham's servant stands and leaves it untouched, telling his errand with earnest gestures. Laban, the aged Bethuel, Rebekah's grey-haired mother and the household sit on rugs listening intently, with Rebekah among them.

Late at night, seen from the starlit courtyard where the camels rest, the wide doorway of Bethuel's house frames the lamplit gathering within. Abraham's servant, one hand on his heart, gestures toward the gold bracelets on Rebekah's wrists as he recounts the meeting at the well, and Laban and the family lean forward, deeply moved, ready to give their answer.

Around a crackling fire in the courtyard of Bethuel's house, Abraham's servant opens cedar chests unloaded from the camels and lays out jewels of silver and gold and fine embroidered garments for Rebekah. Laban and the aged Bethuel look on in agreement, Rebekah's grey-haired mother receives precious gifts, and the whole household gathers round, astonished and glad.

In the cool early morning, camels stand saddled in the courtyard of Bethuel's house and Abraham's servant waits, eager to leave, while Laban and Rebekah's grey-haired mother plead for ten more days. All turn to Rebekah, standing in the doorway in a travelling cloak, who answers with calm resolve that she will go, as pale dawn light spreads over the flat roofs of the city.

Seen from the city wall in bright morning sunshine, Laban and the family stand at the gate with hands raised in blessing as Rebekah rides away on a camel, her old nurse and her maids mounted behind her. Abraham's servant leads the long caravan out across the wide green plain toward the distant hills, a hopeful journey beginning.

At eventide in the open fields of the south country, Isaac walks alone in quiet meditation as a line of camels appears over a low rise against a glowing orange sky. Rebekah slips down from her camel and draws a long veil over her head, while Abraham's servant points across the field toward Isaac, the moment full of expectation.

Under a deep blue night sky full of stars, Isaac gently leads the veiled Rebekah by the hand toward his mother's great tent, its doorway glowing warm with lamplight among the dark tents of the camp. Nearby, Abraham's servant unloads the weary camels, and a sense of peace and comfort settles over the quiet encampment.

On a hazy morning, the very old Abraham stands with Isaac at his side before the great tents, watching as the sons of Keturah, with their wives, children and flocks, set off eastward on camels laden with his parting gifts. Keturah, an older woman in a dark shawl, watches her sons go as the long caravan winds toward the rising sun over the desert hills.

At sunset beneath ancient oaks, the side curtains of Abraham's great tent are rolled up, and Abraham lies peacefully on his couch, at rest after a long and full life. Isaac and Ishmael kneel on either side of him in quiet grief while the household gathers silently outside, and the sky glows gold and rose over the hills.

Seen from a hillside on a grey, still morning, Isaac and Ishmael walk side by side at the head of a funeral procession as servants bear their father's linen-wrapped body on a bier toward the cave of Machpelah at the end of a tree-lined field. A soft radiant beam breaks through the clouds and rests on Isaac, a sign of God's blessing.

Seen from a high ridge under a hot afternoon sky, the black tents, walled towns and hilltop strongholds of Ishmael's people spread across a vast desert toward the horizon. Before the largest tent sits the aged Ishmael, surrounded by his twelve sons, princes in bright robes with their camels and herds, as his long life draws peacefully to its close among them.

On a rocky hilltop above the tents at Lahai-roi under a clear, starry sky, Rebekah, heavy with child and troubled, kneels with her hands lifted, asking the LORD why the babies struggle within her. A shaft of radiant light pours down from the night sky upon her, while far below by the well Isaac kneels in prayer before his tent.

At dawn, the side flaps of a large tent are lifted to the waking camp, and inside in warm lamplight Rebekah rests on cushions, weary and joyful, as two midwives hold up newborn twin boys wrapped in cloths, the first ruddy and covered in reddish hair, the second gripping his brother's heel. Isaac kneels beside her, laughing with wonder.

Seen from a gentle hillside under a bright midday sun, Esau strides in from the open country with his bow and the day's game slung over his shoulder, and Isaac comes out from the tents to greet him with delight. Nearby, Jacob sits quietly in the shade of a tent mending a rope, and Rebekah rests a fond hand on his shoulder.

In the dusty late afternoon under a reddening sky, a clay pot of red lentil stew simmers over a small fire outside Jacob's tent as Jacob, ladle in hand, raises his other hand to make Esau swear. Esau, faint and exhausted from the field, his bow dropped in the dirt, reaches hungrily for the bowl and bread, careless of what he is giving away.

On a parched, famine-struck plain near Gerar at twilight, Isaac's household rests beside thin, weary flocks as the first stars come out. A pillar of radiant light descends before Isaac, who kneels in awe as the voice of the LORD bids him stay in the land and promises him descendants as many as the stars of heaven.

On a sunny afternoon in Gerar, the Philistine king Abimelech, grey-bearded in a crimson robe and gold circlet, looks out in surprise from a low arched window of his palace. Across the garden courtyard, Isaac and Rebekah laugh together beneath a fig tree, his arm around her, plainly husband and wife, though Isaac has called her his sister.

On the pillared portico of Abimelech's palace in Gerar at evening, the king, grey-bearded in a crimson robe, points sternly at Isaac, who stands abashed with Rebekah at his side. Below the steps, Philistine guards and townspeople crowd the square as heralds proclaim the king's command that no one touch this man or his wife.

Seen from a hillside in warm late-morning light, wide fields of ripe barley stretch across the land of Gerar as Isaac's many servants reap heavy sheaves and great flocks and herds graze beyond. Isaac stands among the golden sheaves in wonder as radiant beams break through the clouds over his land, while envious Philistines watch from the ridge.

Under a hazy, overcast sky, Philistine men shovel earth and stones into the old stone-rimmed wells dug long ago, while Abimelech, grey-bearded in a crimson robe, raises his arm and orders Isaac to leave. Isaac turns away calmly, and his long column of laden camels, herds and servants winds down toward the valley of Gerar.

In the hot midday glare of the valley of Gerar, Isaac's servants have reopened the old wells and dug a new one, where fresh water springs up sparkling in the sun. Herdsmen of Gerar push in angrily, shouting and shaking their staffs to claim the water, as Isaac's herdsmen stand their ground and Isaac looks on, troubled, from beside his tent.

Seen from above at golden evening, Isaac's caravan has left a second disputed well behind and come to a broad, open valley where a newly dug well stands quiet, with no one to quarrel over it. Isaac stands beside it with arms opened wide in thankfulness as his tents are pitched and flocks spread out freely across green pasture under a vast, peaceful sky.

At Beer-sheba on a still, moonless night, Isaac kneels before a newly built altar of rough stones, its fire glowing, as a column of radiant light descends from the dark sky and fills the place with brightness. Around him his tents are pitched on the open plain, and servants with lanterns who have begun digging a well nearby pause in awe.

On a hot, windy afternoon at Beer-sheba, Abimelech, grey-bearded in a crimson robe, arrives at Isaac's camp with his richly dressed counsellor Ahuzzath and Phichol, his armoured captain, followed by a small escort of soldiers. Isaac stands wary before his tent, arms folded, as the king opens his hands in a peaceable gesture, asking for a covenant between them.

Seen from a low hill in the fresh early morning at Beer-sheba, the remains of last night's feast lie on rugs before Isaac's tent as Abimelech, in his crimson robe, and his men ride away in peace along the road. At the same moment Isaac's servants run up from a newly dug well, joyfully calling that they have found water, and Isaac turns toward them, glad.

On a grey, overcast day in the camp at Beer-sheba, Esau proudly brings home two Hittite brides, Judith and Bashemath, in bright Canaanite finery and jangling jewellery, followed by their kinsmen bearing gifts. Isaac and Rebekah stand together before their own tent, watching with bowed shoulders and heavy hearts, while the household looks on in uneasy silence.

In the pale light of early dawn, the side curtains of a large tent are rolled up toward the misty hills, and Isaac (old), blind, sits propped on cushions on his couch, reaching out a trembling hand. Esau kneels before him with bow and quiver on his back, listening eagerly as his father asks for savoury venison and promises him the blessing.

Seen from a hillside at mid-morning, behind the tents Rebekah, having overheard, draws Jacob aside near the goat pens and urgently whispers her plan, pointing to two fine young goats in the flock. Jacob spreads his smooth hands in doubt and fear, while far off across the sunlit fields Esau strides away toward the hills with his bow to hunt.

In the smoky cooking place beside the tents at noon, a pot of savoury goat stew steams over the fire and fresh loaves cool on a cloth. Rebekah ties hairy goatskins onto Jacob's hands and the back of his neck as he stands dressed in his brother's fine embroidered robe, uneasy and tense, glancing toward his father's tent.

In the dim, rug-strewn interior of the great tent in the afternoon, shafts of sunlight slant through the open door onto Isaac (old), who sits on his couch and runs his hands doubtfully over the hairy goatskins on Jacob's arms. Jacob kneels before him in his brother's robe, a dish of savoury meat and bread beside him, holding his breath in fear.

Seen from outside at golden late afternoon, the front of the great tent is raised open beside ripening grain fields and vineyards. Within, Isaac (old) lays both hands on the head of Jacob, who kneels before him in his brother's robe beside an emptied dish and wine cup, as the old man solemnly blesses him with the dew of heaven and the fatness of the earth.

Seen from above under a windswept sunset sky, Jacob slips quickly away behind the great tent in his brother's robe just as Esau strides up to the front carrying a steaming dish of venison, his bow on his back. Inside the open doorway, Isaac (old) sits bolt upright on his couch, trembling violently with shock as he realises what has happened.

As dark storm clouds gather at dusk, lamplight spills from the open tent where Esau has fallen to his knees before Isaac (old), arms flung wide and head thrown back, crying out bitterly for a blessing of his own. The old father, shaken and sorrowful, raises a hand over him, while the untouched dish of venison lies on the ground and servants watch from the shadows.

Seen from above on a moonlit night, Esau sits alone on a rocky ridge over the camp, brooding darkly with his bow across his knees and glaring down at the tents. Below, Rebekah has hurried with a small oil lamp to Jacob at his tent door and urges him in a whisper to flee to her brother in Haran, a packed bundle and staff beside him.

At dawn outside the great tent at Beer-sheba, Isaac (old) sits on a stool with his hands raised over Jacob, who kneels before him dressed for a long journey with a staff and a bundle on his shoulder. Rebekah stands close by, tearful but hopeful, and the road north winds away across pale hills beneath a pink and grey morning sky.

At midday among red desert rocks, Esau rides into the encampment of his desert kinsmen, black goat-hair tents pitched among palms around a spring. Before the chief tent, Nebajoth, a bearded desert prince in a striped cloak, presents his veiled sister Mahalath to Esau as a bride, while the tribe gathers to watch and Esau smiles, hoping to please his father.

As the sun sets in a blaze of orange behind barren, rocky hills, Jacob, alone and travel-weary on the road from Beer-sheba toward Haran, sets down his bundle in a wide, stony place and lies down on the hard ground with his head resting on a stone for a pillow, small and solitary under the darkening sky.

In the deep of night on the stony hillside, Jacob sleeps on the ground while a vast, shining stairway rises from beside him up into the starry heavens. Angels climb up and come down its steps, and at its top a brilliant radiance blazes through parted clouds, flooding the sleeping land with golden light as the LORD speaks his promise from the light.

At sunrise on the bare hilltop, Jacob, awed and trembling, has set his stone pillow upright as a plain standing pillar and pours oil from a small flask over its top, the oil glistening in the first rays. Mist lies in the valleys below the stony slopes of Luz as Jacob lifts his eyes to the sky, vowing that this place shall be God's house.

Seen from a low hillside at hazy high noon, three flocks of sheep lie resting on a wide green pasture around a well whose mouth is covered by a great round stone, while their shepherds lounge in the shade of a lone tree. Jacob, travel-worn, leans on his staff and talks with them, and far off across the grass Rachel approaches with her father's flock.

The great round stone lies rolled aside from the well, and Rachel's sheep crowd to drink at the brimming troughs while the astonished shepherds look on. In the warm afternoon light, under drifting white clouds, Jacob, overcome, greets Rachel as his kinswoman with tears of joy, and she stands startled and smiling among her flock, ready to run home with the news.

In the dusty lane before Laban's flat-roofed house at the edge of Haran, Laban, who has come running out in the early evening, throws his arms around Jacob and kisses him in welcome. Rachel, breathless from running, stands by with her sheep, and servants and neighbours look on from the doorways as long golden shadows stretch across the street.

On a breezy spring morning in the courtyard of Laban's house, Laban and Jacob clasp hands over their bargain of seven years of service for Rachel. Rachel stands by the courtyard well with a water jar, glancing shyly at Jacob, while Leah, the elder sister, watches quietly from a doorway, and beyond the walls Laban's flocks spread over the green hills.

On a warm night lit by torches and lanterns, the men of Haran feast and make music at long tables in Laban's courtyard. At the edge of the celebration, Laban leads a bride wrapped from head to foot in a heavy embroidered veil toward the bridal tent, where Jacob waits joyfully, not knowing she is Leah; her young maid Zilpah follows behind.

In the cold grey light of early morning, Jacob has stormed out of the bridal tent and confronts Laban in the courtyard, pointing back in anger and dismay, as Leah stands in the doorway in her bridal robes, veil drawn back and head bowed. Laban, calm and unmoved, spreads his hands with a shrug, while servants clearing the remains of the feast pause to stare.

On a bright, festive afternoon, Laban places Rachel's hand in Jacob's beneath a canopy of woven cloth decked with green branches, Rachel in bridal garments and her young maid Bilhah behind her with a cedar chest. Jacob gazes at Rachel with deep joy, while at the edge of the gathering Leah watches alone in sorrow, and Laban's flocks graze on the hills beyond.

On a mild morning in the family camp near Haran, Leah sits at the door of her tent cradling a newborn son, three small boys playing in the dust around her, and lifts her face in gratitude as a gentle beam of radiant light falls on her tent from the clouds. Across the way, Rachel stands alone at her own tent door, watching with longing.

In the hot, still afternoon among the tents at Haran, Rachel, desperate and in tears, grips Jacob's arm and pleads with him for children while her sister's little sons play noisily nearby. Jacob turns from her in angry frustration, and behind Rachel waits her young maid Bilhah, eyes downcast, whom she will give to Jacob as a wife.

At sunset on a woven mat before her tent, Rachel sits holding Bilhah's newborn son upon her knees, her face bright with triumph, while the young maid Bilhah rests beside her with an older baby boy in her arms. Women of the household gather around to see, and the evening sky glows amber and violet over the camp and the hills of Haran.

On a bright, breezy morning in the open ground between the tents, Leah holds up a newborn boy for all to see, laughing with joy, as the women of the camp gather around her clapping and singing. Her young maid Zilpah sits nearby with another small son on her lap, and Leah's four older boys run about among the goats.

In a golden wheat field at harvest time, with reapers binding sheaves in the late-afternoon sun, Leah's young firstborn son runs up to her holding a bunch of leafy mandrake plants with their yellow fruit. Rachel approaches Leah with an outstretched hand, bargaining for them, and in the distance Jacob walks home from the fields as evening draws near.

Seen from a hillside on a clear spring morning, Leah sits before her tent in the busy camp holding her baby daughter Dinah, while her six sons of different ages gather and play around her, the youngest toddling at her knee. A soft radiant beam breaks through the clouds onto her tent, and Leah lifts her eyes in thankful wonder.

On a still night under a sky full of stars, a column of soft radiant light falls from above onto Rachel's tent, its open doorway glowing. Inside, Rachel, weary but overjoyed, cradles her newborn son wrapped in linen, and Jacob kneels beside her in grateful wonder, while Bilhah and other women of the household gather at the entrance, smiling.

At midday before Laban's house, Jacob stands ready to leave with Rachel, who holds her baby, and Leah, their many children and maids gathered behind them, and points west toward home. Laban, anxious and ingratiating, spreads his hands and pleads with him to stay, while his vast, multiplied flocks and herds cover the surrounding hills under a pale blue sky.

On a cool, cloudy morning in a wide hillside pasture, Laban stands with arms folded as his grown sons drive away every speckled and spotted goat and every brown sheep in a long, dusty stream toward the far hills. Jacob, staff in hand, remains behind with the plain white sheep and dark goats, watching patiently as the herd recedes.

In the late afternoon at a row of stone watering troughs, Jacob sits on a rock peeling bark from green poplar and hazel rods so the white wood shows in stripes. Other striped rods stand in the troughs, where the flocks crowd in to drink before them, and newborn speckled and spotted lambs frisk among them as evening shadows lengthen.

Seen from high above on a hazy summer day, Jacob's own great flocks of streaked, speckled and spotted sheep and goats spread across a broad valley, kept apart from his father-in-law's thinner flocks on the far slopes. Jacob stands on a rise among them, staff in hand, with menservants, maidservants, strings of camels and asses, and a growing camp of tents around him.

Late afternoon on the wide pastures of Padan-aram, seen from a low rise: Jacob stands among his great speckled and spotted flocks while Laban's grown sons mutter and point at him by the stone sheepfold, and Laban watches coldly from his doorway. A radiant beam of golden light breaks through the clouds onto Jacob as the LORD calls him home.

At ground level on a bright morning, in an open field far from their father's house, Jacob has called Rachel and Leah out to his flock; he speaks earnestly, gesturing at the speckled, spotted and striped goats and sheep grazing all around, while the two sisters listen closely beside a lone terebinth tree and gentle hills roll away under a clear blue sky.

column4: The dream of the speckled rams
column7: At night in the open field, Jacob lies asleep on his cloak among his flocks beneath a deep, starry sky; in a dreamlike silver glow, striped, speckled and grizzled rams move through the herd around him, one of the Angels stands beside him in soft white light, and a radiant beam falls from the heavens as the God of Bethel bids him go home.

Seen from a low hill under a high midday sun, Rachel and Leah stand side by side before Jacob in the pasture, resolute, one of them pointing back toward their father's distant mud-brick house; their small children play among the goats nearby, and the wide grassy plain of Padan-aram runs out to a hazy horizon beneath drifting white clouds.

At sunrise outside the tents, Jacob quietly directs his servants as they load the camels and lift Leah and the children onto them, the herds gathered and ready; Rachel slips out of her father's house clutching small clay household idols wrapped in cloth, while far off on a hillside Laban and his men are busy shearing sheep.

An aerial view under a hot midday sun with shimmering haze: Jacob's long caravan fords a broad, shallow river, camels carrying the women and children, flocks and herds splashing through the water as servants drive them on with staffs; Jacob rides at the front, his face set toward the blue hills of Gilead rising on the far side.

column4: God warns Laban in a dream
column7: Deep night in the wooded hills of Gilead: Laban's pursuing band of kinsmen sleeps around dying campfires beside their tethered camels, spears stacked nearby, and in the doorway of the largest tent Laban starts up from his sleep as a radiant column of light pours down from the dark sky upon the camp, warning him not to harm the man he pursues.

On the green slopes of mount Gilead in the fresh morning, two camps of tents face each other across a small valley; Laban strides out ahead of his armed kinsmen with his arms flung wide in reproach, and Jacob stands before his own tents to meet him, while Rachel, Leah and the children watch anxiously from the tent doors.

column4: Wherefore hast thou stolen my gods?
column7: Under a hazy noon sun on the mountainside, Laban demands his stolen household gods, and Jacob, not knowing the truth, sweeps his arm toward his tents to invite a search, before both bands of kinsmen gathered in a wide circle on the grass; behind them, beside her tent, Rachel turns away uneasily.

Seen from above in the afternoon light, the front of Rachel's tent stands open on the mountainside: Laban rummages through baskets, rugs and jars and finds nothing, while Rachel sits calmly on a camel saddle draped with blankets, the stolen images hidden beneath her, excusing herself for not rising; the other tents around stand already searched, their contents scattered.

In the windy late afternoon on mount Gilead, Jacob, angry at last, confronts Laban between the two companies of kinsmen, who stand on either side as judges; Laban's searched belongings lie spread on the ground between them, and Jacob points with his weathered shepherd's staff to the flocks on the hillside, recalling twenty years of scorching days and frosty nights.

Under gathering evening clouds on the mountain, Jacob sets upright a tall standing stone while his kinsmen and Laban's carry stones and pile them into a great heap beside it; Laban looks on, his anger spent, and the men sit down together on the heap to share bread as the light fades over the folded hills.

At sunset on the ridge of Gilead, seen from slightly below, Laban and Jacob stand facing each other on either side of the stone heap and the tall pillar, each raising a hand to swear a covenant of peace, their kinsmen gathered behind them; the sky blazes orange and violet over the wide valleys that will now lie between them.

Early morning mist fills the valleys below mount Gilead; smoke from Jacob's sacrifice still curls up from a stone altar on the summit, and Laban kisses and blesses his daughters Rachel and Leah and their children while Jacob stands by; Laban's camel and kinsmen wait to carry him down the slope toward home.

In golden late-afternoon light on a quiet road through hill country, Jacob's caravan halts in wonder: on the slopes on both sides stand ranks of Angels, men in white with a soft light about them, like a great encamped host; Jacob stands before his camels at the head of the column, gazing up at them in awe.

From a rocky height on a bright, breezy morning, Jacob sends off a small band of messengers on donkeys with a humble greeting for his brother; they set off down a winding road that leads far to the south, where the red mountains of Seir glow on the hazy horizon, while Jacob's tents and herds spread across the valley behind him.

Under a darkening, stormy sky, the messengers have hurried back with news that his brother is coming with four hundred men; Jacob, afraid, stands in the middle of a broad valley directing his servants to split the people, flocks, herds and camels into two separate companies, one driven off to the left and one to the right.

At twilight, Jacob kneels alone on a flat rock above the valley with his hands lifted to the sky in prayer, his old shepherd's staff lying beside him; below, the fires of his two camps flicker in the dusk, and the first stars are appearing above the hills, countless like the sand of the sea.

Under a bright moon, with torches flaring, Jacob walks with his herdsmen among a great gathering of animals, choosing his gift for his brother: hundreds of goats and ewes, rams, milk camels with their colts, cows and bulls, she-asses and foals, which busy servants sort into separate brushwood pens across the camp.

An aerial view in early morning of a long road winding across dry, golden hills: drove after drove of goats, sheep, camels, cattle and donkeys moves along it toward the south, each with its own herdsman and a wide gap before the next, while far behind, at the edge of the camp, Jacob stands watching them go.

In the dead of night under a pale moon, Jacob leads Rachel and Leah, their two maidservants and his eleven sons across the shallow ford of the Jabbok, a rocky stream deep in a gorge; torchlight glints on the dark water as servants carry the little ones and the baggage over to the far bank.

Alone on the stony bank of the Jabbok in the last dark hour before dawn, Jacob wrestles with a mysterious man, one of the Angels, in white with a soft glow about him, the two locked together among the boulders; Jacob, his hip wrenched out of joint, still clings on and will not let go as the first grey light touches the eastern hills.

As day breaks over the gorge of the Jabbok, the man in white, one of the Angels, glowing softly, lays his hands on Jacob and blesses him with a new name as Jacob kneels on the riverbank; a radiant golden light floods down from the opening sky over the whole place, Peniel, where Jacob has seen God face to face and lived.

Seen from the far slope, the sun rises gold over the hills as Jacob, alone, limps up out of the river gorge, leaning heavily on his staff and favouring his hip; ahead of him his family's tents and camels wait in the morning light, and the Jabbok glitters in the valley below.

Seen from a rise behind Jacob's company on a wide open plain at mid-morning, a dust cloud rolls in from the horizon where Esau approaches with four hundred men; Jacob hurriedly arranges his household in ranks, the two handmaids and their children in front, Leah and her children behind them, and Rachel with her small son last of all.

At ground level in the middle of the sunlit plain, Jacob, who has come forward bowing to the ground seven times, is caught up in Esau's embrace as Esau runs to him, and the two brothers weep on each other's necks; behind Jacob, Rachel, Leah and the children wait in a long line, and behind Esau his four hundred men stand beside their camels.

Seen from a little above on the grassy plain beneath a wide blue sky with a few high clouds, the handmaids and their children come forward and bow low before Esau, then Leah with her sons and daughter, and last Rachel with her little boy; Esau looks on, moved, as Jacob stands beside him presenting each of them.

In the warm early afternoon beside a grove of feathery tamarisks, Jacob urges Esau to accept his present, gesturing toward the great droves of goats, sheep, camels and cattle grazing across the plain behind them; Esau, who first raised a hand to refuse, now clasps Jacob's arm and accepts, both of them smiling.

From a hilltop in the late afternoon, the road below forks: Esau and his four hundred men ride away south toward the red mountains of Seir, Esau turning back to wave, while Jacob's slow company of children, ewes and newborn lambs heads the other way, down toward a green valley at Succoth where his men are raising booths of leafy branches.

Seen from across the valley in the evening light, the walled hill city of Shechem glows golden; in a green field before its gate Jacob's tents are pitched, and Jacob sets the last stones on a new altar as his family gathers around, while a man of the city walks off with the bag of silver paid for the field.

Bright morning outside the walled city of Shechem: Dinah, a young girl in a simple blue dress and headscarf, walks from her family's tents toward a well where the local girls gather with water jars, and up at the city gate, among his attendants, the prince Shechem, a young man in rich embroidered robes, stands watching her.

Late afternoon at the tents on the hillside below Shechem: Jacob sits silent and grieving at his tent door, while Joseph's brothers, Jacob's grown sons, stride in from the fields with their staffs, furious at the news, and from the city gate below, Hamor, an elderly Hivite prince in rich robes, comes walking up with his attendants to speak with Jacob.

In the heat of the day beneath a wide awning before Jacob's tent, Hamor and his son Shechem, a young prince in fine robes, plead with Jacob and Joseph's brothers, offering marriage, land and trade; servants have set out chests, rich cloth, jars and silver on a carpet as gifts, while the stern brothers stand with arms folded.

In golden evening light, seen from a little above, Joseph's brothers stand together in a line before their tents and answer Hamor and Shechem calmly but craftily, setting them a hard condition; the eager father and son nod their agreement and turn back toward the walled city glowing on its hill, while the brothers exchange knowing looks.

Under a hazy midday sky, the men of Shechem crowd the broad stone-paved square inside the city gate, listening as Hamor and his son Shechem, standing on the gate's steps in their fine robes, urge them to make peace and become one people with the shepherd family camped outside the walls; across the crowd, heads nod in agreement.

column4: Simeon and Levi bring Dinah out
