column7: At dusk on the third day, under a darkening red sky, Simeon and Levi lead their sister Dinah out through the silent city gate, swords sheathed at their sides, as the rest of Joseph's brothers drive the city's sheep, oxen and laden donkeys out behind them; the town on the hill stands hushed and empty, with no one in its streets.

Night has fallen over the hills; by the light of a campfire among the tents, Jacob, distressed, rebukes Simeon and Levi, pointing out toward the distant lights of the Canaanite towns on the surrounding hills, while the two stand defiant and the rest of Joseph's brothers look on in silence.

Morning under a great oak outside Shechem: Jacob kneels at its roots burying a heap of small idols and earrings, while his household stands by in clean, fresh garments beside loaded camels, ready to go up to Bethel; a radiant shaft of light falls from the clouds onto the oak, and on the far hills the walled towns look on in fear.

On an overcast afternoon at Bethel, Jacob and his household stand weeping beneath a huge spreading oak at the foot of a stony hill, gathered around a fresh grave of piled stones where old Deborah, the family's aged nurse, has been laid to rest; on the rocky summit above stands the new stone altar Jacob has built, a thin thread of smoke rising.

At Bethel in the stillness of dawn, a great pillar of radiant light descends through a parting in the clouds onto the rocky hilltop, and Jacob kneels before it with arms raised as God blesses him and confirms his new name; his camp lies small in the valley below, and the promised land stretches away in every direction.

Mid-morning on the hilltop of Bethel, the radiant light withdraws upward into the bright clouds as Jacob pours oil and a drink offering from a clay jar over a tall standing stone he has set up; his family watches reverently from the slope below, and the hills around lie bathed in clear sunshine.

At dusk on the open road near Ephrath, a tent has been hastily pitched by the wayside; through its open front Rachel lies weak on cushions with Jacob kneeling at her side, while the midwife steps out cradling a newborn son wrapped in cloth and the rest of the family waits anxiously by the camels under the darkening sky.

On a windswept grey morning beside the road to Bethlehem, Jacob, bowed with grief and holding his swaddled newborn son, stands before a fresh grave on which he has raised a tall stone pillar; Leah and the children stand behind him, and the road winds on toward a little town on a distant hill.

On a broad green pasture beyond a tall stone watchtower, Jacob's tents spread among grazing flocks in clear afternoon light; before them his twelve sons gather around him, Joseph's brothers from the eldest down, then Joseph (youth) and a baby carried by a nurse, while their mothers Leah, Bilhah and Zilpah stand among the tents.

At sunset among the great oaks of Mamre near Hebron, Esau and Jacob stand side by side at the sealed mouth of a cave tomb in the hillside, mourning their aged father, who has died old and full of days; their households stand in silence behind them, long shadows stretching across the golden grass.

An aerial view in bright morning light of Esau's great household on the move: Esau rides at the head, followed by his wives, sons and daughters on camels, servants and vast herds of cattle and goats, the long column winding away from the green hills of Canaan into the towering red sandstone mountains of Seir.

column4: Esau's sons, the dukes of Edom
column7: In a wide valley among the red rock mountains of Edom at midday, Esau sits as patriarch before his great tent, surrounded by his sons and grandsons, the chieftains of Edom, in rich robes with staffs of office, each with his own clan, tents and herds spreading out across the valley floor.

Late afternoon in the canyons of Seir: the Horites, the old people of the land, live in dwellings carved into towering red cliffs, and their chiefs stand gathered on a ledge before their cave homes; in the wilderness below, a young herdsman tending his father's donkeys stops in wonder at a herd of mules he has found among the rocks.

column4: The kings and dukes of Edom
column7: At dusk, a long procession of the kings of Edom, one after another through the generations, each crowned and robed, winds along a road through red rock gorges toward a fortified city of red stone on a crag, followed by the clan chiefs and their people, torches beginning to glow against the purple sky.

In the green vale of Hebron on a bright spring morning, Jacob drapes a splendid coat of many colours over the shoulders of Joseph (youth) before the family tents, beaming with love; a short way off, Joseph's brothers, back from the flocks with their staffs, stand together scowling at the sight.

At harvest in a golden wheat field under a hot afternoon sun, Joseph (youth), in his coat of many colours, stands telling his dream while Joseph's brothers, binding sheaves, straighten up and glare at him; around them bound sheaves stand in the stubble in a wide ring, one standing tall in the middle, just as in the dream.

Evening at the tents in Hebron: Joseph (youth) stands by the fire telling his second dream to his father and brothers, pointing up at a deepening sky where the sun's last glow, a bright moon and eleven brilliant stars shine together; Jacob, seated, raises a hand in rebuke yet looks thoughtful, while Joseph's brothers sit apart, bitter and envious.

Early morning in the vale of Hebron, mist lifting from the olive groves: Jacob stands at the door of his tent with a hand raised in farewell as Joseph (youth), in his coat of many colours, with a staff and a bag of provisions, sets off along the path that winds north through the hills.

Under a cloudy, windswept sky on wide, empty grazing lands near Shechem, with mountains rising behind, Joseph (youth), alone in his bright coat, wanders in search of his brothers, and a local farmer leaning on his hoe points him onward to the north, toward Dothan; no flocks are anywhere in sight, only grass, stone walls and scattered trees.

Seen from behind them on a rocky hillside at Dothan in the clear late morning, Joseph's brothers huddle together, plotting, as the small bright figure of Joseph (youth) in his colourful coat approaches far off across the plain; Reuben stands among them with a hand raised, urging them to spare him, and nearby gapes the dark mouth of a dry cistern.

Seen from above under a harsh, white midday sun in the wilderness, Joseph's brothers stand around the mouth of a dry stone cistern, one of them holding up the coat of many colours; below, at the bottom of the empty pit, Joseph (youth), stripped to his plain undertunic, looks up at them in dismay.

column4: Sold for twenty pieces of silver
column7: In the late afternoon at Dothan, a caravan of merchants with camels laden with spices, balm and myrrh has halted beside the pit on its way down to Egypt; Joseph (youth) is hauled up from the pit with a rope while Judah takes twenty pieces of silver from the caravan's leader, and the rest of Joseph's brothers, their meal of bread left on a rock, look on.

At dusk the empty plain at Dothan lies in long blue shadows; Reuben stands alone at the mouth of the empty cistern, tearing his clothes in grief, while far off on the horizon a line of camels disappears toward the south and his brothers' campfire glows on a distant rise.

At the tents in Hebron on a grey, overcast day, Joseph's brothers have come home, and one of them holds up the torn coat of many colours before their father; Jacob, recognizing it, staggers back with his hands raised in horror, while the other brothers stand in a silent row with lowered eyes.

Soft rain falls over the vale of Hebron; Jacob, his clothes torn and sackcloth about his waist, sits on the ground before his tent in mourning, turning away from Joseph's brothers and their sisters, who kneel around him trying to comfort him, while far down the southern road a tiny caravan fades into the haze toward Egypt.

On green terraced hills near Adullam in soft morning light, Judah stands outside his new stone house with his Canaanite wife, a young woman in a red-striped dress, and their three small sons playing at their feet, while his friend Hirah the Adullamite, a stocky herdsman in a striped cloak, comes up the path with a basket of figs.

Under heavy grey clouds, Tamar, a slender young woman in dark widow's garments, walks away from Judah's house along a hill road toward her father's home, leading a donkey with her belongings; on the slope above stand two fresh stone grave cairns, and Judah watches from his doorway beside his youngest son, a boy.

On a bright spring day at a crossroads beside a small town gate on the hilly road to Timnath, Tamar, her widow's clothes put away and her face hidden by a long veil, sits alone on a stone in the open; far down the road, Judah and his friend Hirah walk up toward the sheep-shearing on the hills, where flocks crowd the pens.

By the roadside near the town gate in the warm afternoon, Judah, not knowing that the veiled woman is Tamar, hands her his signet seal on its cord, his bracelets and his carved staff as a pledge for a young goat he promises to send; she sits wrapped in her long veil on the stone, and the road runs on into the hills.

In the cool evening light at the town gate on the Timnath road, Hirah the Adullamite, a stocky herdsman in a striped cloak, leads a young goat on a cord to the empty roadside spot and asks the old townsmen seated by the gate, who shake their heads; far along the road behind him, a woman in dark widow's garments walks quietly home.

column4: She is more righteous than I
column7: At the gate of Judah's town under a hot noon sky, a crowd of townsmen has brought Tamar out, and her messenger lays a signet seal, bracelets and a staff before Judah, who stands at the front of the crowd staring at his own belongings, ashamed, and raises his hand to halt them, declaring her more righteous than himself.

In the shaded courtyard of a stone house on a fresh morning, Tamar rests on cushions beneath a fig tree, smiling, while the midwife holds up two newborn twin boys wrapped in linen, a scarlet thread tied around the wrist of one; women of the household gather around rejoicing, and green hills rise beyond the courtyard wall.

At a busy market on the bank of the Nile under a blazing midday sky, Potiphar, captain of the royal guard, pays the Ishmaelite traders for Joseph, who stands among their camels; a soft beam of radiant light rests on Joseph, while around them Egyptians bustle with goods and sailing boats crowd the river beneath palm trees and temple walls.

Seen from above in the late afternoon, Potiphar's estate by the Nile flourishes: Joseph, now overseer, directs Egyptians of the household carrying baskets of grain, fruit and jars through a courtyard of painted columns, while fields and orchards beyond overflow with harvest; Potiphar rests contented on a shaded terrace, and a warm golden glow from heaven lies over the whole house.

In a lofty hall of painted columns opening onto a garden, with morning sunlight slanting between the pillars, the master's wife, an elegant Egyptian lady in a pleated linen gown and jewelled collar, beckons to Joseph from her carved chair; Joseph, carrying a basket of folded linens, stands well back, shaking his head and raising a hand in firm refusal.

At noon the great house stands empty of servants; Joseph runs out through the tall doorway into the bright garden in his plain linen tunic, fleeing, while in the shadowed hall behind him the master's wife stands holding his outer cloak in her hands; palm trees and a lotus pool shimmer in the sun.

At dusk, torches flare at the gate of the house as Potiphar returns home with his guards; his wife stands in the courtyard holding up the Hebrew servant's cloak as proof, crying out her false story, while Egyptians of the household crowd around her and Potiphar stops short, listening with a darkening face.

In the cold grey light of early morning, Potiphar strides grimly ahead as Egyptians of his guard march Joseph, his hands bound, across a dusty square toward the massive mud-brick walls of the king's prison, whose heavy wooden gate stands open; beyond the walls the city is only beginning to wake.

Inside the high-walled courtyard of the prison on a dim afternoon, a shaft of radiant light falls from above onto Joseph as he moves among the Egyptians held there, seeing to their bread and water; the keeper of the prison, a heavy-set jailer with keys at his belt, watches with approval from a shaded doorway, content to leave everything in his hands.

Seen from above, in the walled prison yard of the captain of the guard's house, late afternoon sun slants across mud-brick walls; Potiphar hands two disgraced royal officers, Pharaoh's chief butler and chief baker, still in fine court linen, into Joseph's care, and Joseph, a prisoner in a plain tunic, bows to receive them as guards swing the heavy gate shut.

Early morning light falls through a high barred window into a long stone prison hall, where the butler and the baker sit slumped on their sleeping mats, troubled by the dreams of the night; Joseph, carrying a water jar, stops before them and gently asks why they look so sad, opening his hand as if to say interpretations belong to God.

column4: The butler's dream of the vine
column7: A dream bathed in soft golden haze: the chief butler stands in a glowing vineyard before a vine with three branches that bud, blossom and hang heavy with ripe purple grapes all at once; he presses the grapes into Pharaoh's golden cup and holds it out to Pharaoh, seated on a throne half-seen in the mist.

At midday in the dim prison hall, a shaft of dusty light falls between Joseph and the chief butler while other prisoners rest along the walls; Joseph holds up three fingers for the three days, and the butler's face lifts with hope, as Joseph, his other hand on his heart, begs to be remembered before Pharaoh.

Another dream, under a heavy, darkening sky: the chief baker walks along a dusty road across a bare plain with three white wicker baskets stacked on his head, the top one heaped with breads and pastries for Pharaoh, while a flock of black birds swoops down to peck at them and he cannot drive them away; the whole scene feels ominous.

Seen from a high gallery, Pharaoh's birthday feast fills a great hall of lotus-painted columns with lamplight, music and laden tables; on his throne Pharaoh takes a golden cup from the restored chief butler, who bows and smiles, while across the hall guards lead the chief baker away through a doorway into the dusk, and the happy butler has already forgotten the prison.

In a strange dream at dawn, Pharaoh stands alone among tall reeds on the bank of the broad Nile; seven sleek, fat cows climb out of the river and graze in a lush meadow, while seven gaunt, bony cows rise from the water behind them and close in menacingly under a sickly yellow sky.

Pharaoh's second dream: across a vast field under a white-hot midday sun, one tall stalk bears seven plump golden ears of grain, while beside it seven thin, scorched ears spring up, bent by a fierce east wind that drives dust over the land; small amid the stalks, Pharaoh stands shading his eyes, troubled.

Morning in Pharaoh's vast throne hall: a row of magicians and wise men in white linen and leopard skins stand with lowered heads, unable to explain the dreams, while Pharaoh sits troubled on his throne between lotus-painted columns; from among the courtiers, the chief butler steps forward with a raised hand, suddenly remembering the young Hebrew in the prison.

Seen from the tall doorway behind him, Joseph, just brought in haste from the dungeon, freshly shaven and in clean white linen, stands humbly at the foot of the steps before Pharaoh on his throne, hands open, saying the answer will come from God; courtiers crowd both sides of the bright hall, staring at the young Hebrew prisoner.

Seen from high among the painted columns of the throne hall in late morning, Pharaoh leans forward on his throne and recounts his two dreams with urgent, troubled gestures, while Joseph stands alone below on the patterned floor, listening intently, and the courtiers wait in silence along the walls in shafts of dusty sunlight.

column4: Seven years of plenty and famine
column7: On a high palace terrace in the bright afternoon, Joseph stands before Pharaoh's chair and points out over the Nile valley stretching into the distance: near the river the fields shine green and gold, while far off a brown haze of dust hangs over the desert horizon; Pharaoh and his courtiers listen in hushed awe.

Late afternoon in the throne hall: Joseph scoops a handful of golden wheat from a tall basket and lets it pour back as he counsels Pharaoh to store up a fifth of every harvest in the cities; Pharaoh, chin in hand, considers, and his officials lean in, nodding, as long shadows stretch across the painted floor.

Seen from the far end of the hall, Pharaoh rises from his golden throne and comes down the steps toward Joseph with one hand stretched out to him, as the courtiers and servants lining the hall exchange astonished looks and murmur their approval; low evening sun pours in between the painted columns and falls on Joseph, who bows his head in wonder.

Seen from high above a sunlit morning avenue lined with sphinxes and palms, Joseph rides in Pharaoh's second chariot behind prancing horses, robed in fine linen, a gold chain at his neck and Pharaoh's ring on his hand; runners ahead cry out, the crowds on both sides fall to their knees, and Pharaoh watches from the palace gate.

In the courtyard of the sun temple at On in the golden evening, beneath tall smooth obelisks and a rose-tinted sky, Pharaoh gives Joseph a new Egyptian name and presents to him Asenath, the priest's daughter, in a pleated white gown; her father Poti-pherah stands beside them in priestly robes as Joseph takes her hand before the gathered court.

Seen from a hillside at harvest time, the Nile valley overflows with golden wheat; at the edge of a walled city, Joseph stands in his chariot overseeing long lines of workers who carry baskets of grain up ramps into rows of domed granaries, where the grain is heaped like sand dunes, too much to count, in the bright morning light.

At dusk in the garden of Joseph's house, beside a lotus pool, Joseph lifts his newborn second son toward the evening sky in thanks, while his wife Asenath sits on a cushioned bench cradling their little firstborn; servants light lamps among the palms, and the whole garden glows with quiet joy and peace.

Under a scorching white sky, the fields along the shrunken Nile lie cracked and barren; a great crowd of hungry Egyptians, gaunt families holding up empty baskets, presses against the palace gates crying for bread, and Pharaoh, on a high balcony, stretches out his arm toward the distant domed granaries, telling them to go to the governor.

At sunrise the great doors of the granaries stand open and Joseph, on a raised platform, directs officials pouring out grain into the sacks of buyers; seen from above, long lines of Egyptians and caravans of foreigners from many lands, with camels and donkeys, stretch back across the dusty plain as far as the eye can see.

In the dry hill country of Canaan, under a pale dawn sky, the ten brothers load empty sacks onto their donkeys beside Jacob's tents and set off down the rocky path toward Egypt; Jacob stands at the tent door with his hand firmly on Benjamin's shoulder, keeping him at home, his face full of worry.

In a vast granary courtyard crowded with buyers from many lands, in the late-morning glare, Joseph sits on a raised seat under a striped awning, officials and guards around him; before him the ten dusty brothers from Canaan bow down with their faces to the ground, not knowing him, while Joseph gazes at them, knowing them at once.

Seen from the granary roof, Joseph rises from his seat and points sternly at the brothers, speaking harshly through an interpreter, as Egyptian guards with spears close in around them; the ten men kneel in the dust of the courtyard with hands spread wide, protesting that they are honest sons of one man, while the hot noon sun beats down on the crowded square.

On the third morning the heavy door of a stone guardhouse swings open and cool grey light falls across the ten brothers sitting on the straw-strewn floor; Joseph stands in the doorway with guards behind him, offering them terms: one brother stays bound while the rest carry grain home to their hungry families and bring back the youngest.

Under an overcast sky in a walled courtyard, the brothers huddle in anguish, confessing their guilt over the brother they sold, as Reuben reproaches them with raised hands; a little apart, Joseph has turned away behind a column to weep unseen, while Egyptian guards bind Simeon's wrists with cords before his brothers' eyes.

Seen from a high wall, servants in the busy yard of the royal granary fill the brothers' sacks to the brim with golden grain and quietly slip pouches of silver into the mouth of each sack; the nine brothers load their donkeys and lead them out through the tall city gate into the hot afternoon glare, leaving Simeon behind.

At a lonely lodging place on the desert road, under a starry night sky, a small fire lights the camp where the donkeys stand tethered; one brother, opening his sack to feed his donkey, holds up a pouch of silver glinting in the firelight, and the others crowd around him, pale with fear, asking what God has done to them.

Back in the brown hills of Canaan at midday, the brothers sit in a circle with Jacob in the shade of a great terebinth tree beside his tents, their laden donkeys resting nearby; they tell him everything the stern lord of Egypt said, gesturing toward the south, while Jacob listens gravely, missing Simeon, with Benjamin seated close at his side.

In the lamplit evening under the open front of Jacob's great tent, the brothers empty their grain sacks onto woven mats and find a bundle of silver in every heap; Jacob, stricken with grief, holds Benjamin close and turns away, mourning Joseph and Simeon, while Reuben kneels before him with outstretched hands, pledging his own two sons to bring Benjamin back.

Seen from a rocky slope above the camp, under a blazing sun in drought-stricken Canaan, empty grain jars stand beside Jacob's tents and thin flocks wander over bare, cracked earth; Jacob urges his sons to go back to Egypt for food, but Judah stands before him shaking his head, palms open, reminding him of the man's warning, while the other brothers sit in the scant shade.

In the cool of evening at the edge of the camp, as the sun sinks behind the hills, Judah rests a protective hand on Benjamin's shoulder and lays his other hand on his heart before Jacob, solemnly vowing to bear the blame forever if he does not bring Benjamin home; Jacob, leaning on his staff, searches his son's face.

column4: Gifts for the man in Egypt
column7: At dawn outside Jacob's tents, the brothers load their donkeys with gifts for the lord of Egypt: jars of balm and honey, bundles of spices and myrrh, baskets of nuts and almonds, and pouches of double silver; Jacob raises his hands in blessing over them and lets Benjamin go with them, his face heavy with sorrow.

In the crowded granary hall of Egypt at mid-morning, the brothers stand before Joseph with their gifts and double silver, Benjamin among them; Joseph, seated in state, catches sight of Benjamin and turns to his steward, ordering a noon feast to be prepared, and the steward leads the uneasy brothers away toward Joseph's grand house.

Seen from across a palm-shaded forecourt, the frightened brothers press around the steward at the tall doorway of Joseph's house, holding out their bags of silver and pleading that they never stole it; the steward smiles and raises a calming hand, and behind him a servant leads Simeon out into the sunlight to rejoin his astonished brothers.

In a cool inner courtyard of Joseph's house, with a fountain splashing among palm trees in the bright noon light, servants bring basins of water and the brothers wash their dusty feet while their donkeys eat fodder by the wall; Benjamin and the others carefully lay out their gifts of balm, honey and almonds, waiting nervously for Joseph.

Seen from a high gallery of Joseph's hall, Joseph enters through tall doors and the brothers kneel and bow to the tiled floor before him, holding out their gifts; he asks after the health of their old father, and they bow their heads again as they answer, the gifts of balm, honey and spices spread between them.

In a small private chamber off the great hall, lit by a single shaft of light from a high window, Joseph bends over a stone basin, weeping for his brother Benjamin; through the half-open door the brothers can be seen waiting in the bright hall beyond, Benjamin among them, while a servant stands outside holding a linen towel.

Seen from the end of a long banquet hall lit by lamps and high windows, three tables stand apart: Joseph dines alone on a raised dais, the Egyptians at their own table, and the eleven brothers sit in order from eldest to youngest, staring at one another in amazement; servants carry heaped platters, Benjamin's five times larger, as the brothers begin to laugh and drink.

Late at night in a lamp-lit storeroom stacked with bulging grain sacks, Joseph hands his silver drinking cup to his steward, who tucks it quietly into the mouth of the youngest brother's sack beside his money; through the open doorway, the brothers' donkeys stand tethered in the moonlit courtyard, ready for the morning.

Seen from high above at first light, the brothers' little caravan of laden donkeys winds along a desert road beyond the city walls under a pink and gold sky; behind them a plume of dust rises as Joseph's steward and his horsemen gallop to overtake them, and the brothers turn in alarm as he calls out his accusation.

On the open road under a clear morning sky, with the distant city walls still in view, the brothers stand around the mounted steward and his horsemen, spreading their hands and shaking their heads in protest; so sure are they of their innocence that they swear whoever has the cup shall die, and the rest become slaves.

Under the harsh midday sun, the sacks lie opened along the dusty roadside as the steward searches from the eldest to the youngest; he lifts the gleaming silver cup out of Benjamin's sack, Benjamin stands stunned, and his brothers tear their cloaks in grief, some already turning their laden donkeys back toward the city.

In the early afternoon shade of Joseph's great hall, the brothers in their torn garments throw themselves face down on the stone floor before Joseph, who stands stern beside his seat holding the silver cup; Judah lifts his head to confess that they are all his servants now, and Benjamin kneels among them with a guard at his side.

column5: Judah, Joseph (governor), Joseph's brothers, Benjamin, Egyptians
column7: Seen from behind the kneeling brothers, Judah rises and steps close to Joseph's raised seat, bowing low with his hands pressed together as he begs leave to speak; the hall is hushed in the slanting afternoon light, the others kneel in a row in their torn clothes, and Benjamin stands between two Egyptian guards with his head bowed.

Seen from high in the hall, Judah stands alone at the centre of the polished floor, his hands open and trembling as he tells of their father's grief for the son torn in pieces and his dread of losing Benjamin; Joseph sits motionless on his seat, his face half turned away, as long golden beams of evening light fall across the kneeling brothers.

Seen at floor level from the side of the hall as servants light the lamps at dusk, Judah kneels at the foot of Joseph's dais with one arm stretched toward Benjamin, offering to stay as a slave in his place so that Benjamin may go home to their father; the brothers look on in tears, and Joseph grips the arm of his seat, close to breaking.

Seen from the far end of the lamp-lit hall, the last Egyptian servants hurry out through the tall doors at Joseph's command; alone with his brothers, Joseph stands with his arms spread wide, weeping aloud as he cries out that he is Joseph, and the eleven brothers stagger back in shock and fear, unable to answer.

Joseph beckons, and his frightened brothers edge toward him across the hall, where moonlight now joins the lamplight through the high windows; he stretches out his hands and speaks tenderly, telling them not to grieve over selling him, for God sent him ahead to save lives, and they gaze at him in wonder as the truth sinks in.

At sunrise on a palace terrace high above the river, Joseph points north toward the green, well-watered pastures of Goshen glowing in the distance, urging his brothers to hurry home and bring their father down with all his flocks and herds; Benjamin stands close at his side, and the brothers gaze out over the rich land in astonishment.

Seen from above on the bright morning terrace, Joseph throws his arms around Benjamin's neck and the two brothers weep on each other's shoulders; then one by one he embraces and kisses the others, their fear melting into tears and eager talk, while below them the rooftops of the city and the shining Nile spread out to the horizon.

In Pharaoh's palace garden at midday, beside a pool of blue lotus flowers, a delighted Pharaoh speaks with Joseph while his pleased servants look on; beyond the garden wall, rows of sturdy wooden wagons are being readied with teams of oxen, to bring Joseph's father, the wives and the little ones from Canaan to the good of the land.

Seen from high above the city gate at dawn, a long caravan sets out across the plain: Egyptian wagons, ten donkeys laden with the good things of Egypt and ten more with grain and bread; the brothers in new garments wave farewell, Benjamin with a heavy bag of silver, while Joseph stands at the gate calling after them not to quarrel on the way.

On a windswept hilltop in Canaan at sunset, Jacob stands at the door of his tent as his sons run up to tell him that Joseph is alive, the Egyptian wagons rolling up the slope behind them; at first he sways in disbelief, steadied by Benjamin, but at the sight of the wagons his spirit revives and he lifts his staff toward Egypt.

At night by the wells of Beer-sheba, with the caravan's wagons and tents dark in the background, Jacob kneels beside a stone altar where his sacrifice still smoulders; a radiant beam of light pours down from the starry sky and surrounds him as God speaks in a vision, telling him not to fear going down into Egypt.

column4: Into Egypt with all his seed
column7: Seen from a high ridge in the morning, a great caravan stretches across the desert toward Egypt: Pharaoh's wagons carry Jacob, the wives and the little children, followed by flocks of sheep and goats, herds of cattle and donkeys laden with goods, while Jacob's sons walk alongside and the long line raises golden dust into the sunlight.

At ground level on the wilderness road at midday, Reuben, Judah and the other sons of Leah walk at the head of their own households, each family a cluster of wives, sons, grandsons and daughters around their wagons and donkeys, with Dinah among them; the long procession of thirty-three souls winds through a dry, rocky wadi under a pale blue sky.

column4: The families of Zilpah and Rachel
column7: At night the caravan camps at a desert oasis among tall date palms under a sky full of stars; around glowing cooking fires gather the families of Gad and Asher, and Benjamin sits among his ten sons while children chase one another between the firelit tents, the whole clan resting together on the road to Egypt.

An aerial view at sunset as the whole house of Jacob, with its wagons, flocks and herds, reaches the green edge of the Nile delta, the desert behind turning violet; Jacob rides at the front in a wagon surrounded by his sons and grandsons, and the families of Dan and Naphtali bring up the rear of the long, winding line.

In the green pastures of Goshen on a bright morning, Joseph's gilded chariot stands abandoned on the road as he holds his father in his arms beside the family's wagon, and the two weep on each other's necks a long while; Judah, the brothers and their families stand back among the grazing flocks, moved to tears.

Seen from a low hill in the late afternoon, Joseph stands among his brothers and their grazing flocks on the wide pastures of Goshen, explaining how they must answer Pharaoh: they are to say they have kept cattle from their youth, as their fathers did; the brothers listen, leaning on their shepherd's staffs, as long shadows stretch across the grass.

On a bright morning in Pharaoh's splendid throne hall, five of Joseph's brothers in rough shepherds' cloaks stand a little awkwardly on the polished floor among richly dressed courtiers, staffs in hand, telling Pharaoh they are shepherds; Joseph stands beside them, and Pharaoh, leaning forward on his throne, opens his hand graciously, granting them the land of Goshen.

In the golden evening light of the palace hall, with Joseph at his side, Jacob leans on his shepherd's staff and raises his hand in blessing over Pharaoh, who has risen respectfully from his throne to ask his age; courtiers watch in silence, the humble old shepherd blessing the mightiest king on earth.

Seen from above on a peaceful morning, the fertile land of Goshen spreads green beside a branch of the Nile, dotted with new tents, sheepfolds and grazing herds; Joseph walks among the families with servants carrying baskets of bread, handing loaves to the brothers' wives and children, while Jacob sits contentedly at the door of his tent.

In the parched heat of the famine, under a hazy copper sky, people from Egypt and Canaan pay for grain at a royal storehouse, where officials weigh heaps of silver on great balance scales; porters carry chests of silver up the steps of Pharaoh's treasury while Joseph oversees the work from a shaded portico, and beyond, the fields lie brown and dead.

On the dusty plain outside a granary city in the early morning, crowds of hungry Egyptians lead their horses, flocks, cattle and donkeys toward Joseph, who stands on the granary steps directing his men to hand out bread in exchange; seen from a nearby rooftop, the animals fill wide pens while people carry loaves away in their arms.

Under a dull, dust-laden sky a year later, a great crowd of gaunt Egyptian farmers kneels before Joseph at the edge of their barren, cracked fields, offering their land and themselves to Pharaoh for bread; Joseph listens gravely from his chariot, while in the distance white-robed priests stand apart by their temple, whose land is not sold.

Seen from a low hillside in fresh morning light, Joseph hands sacks of seed to farmers on the dark, damp soil of the Nile floodplain, and they bow gratefully, saying he has saved their lives; around them families have begun sowing again, scattering seed in long rows under a clear sky, as hope returns to the land.

column4: Swear to bury me in Canaan
column7: Years later, Goshen is thronged with Israel's growing families and flocks; in a spacious house whose open side looks out on the evening pastures, Jacob lies propped on his bed, gripping Joseph's hand as Joseph kneels beside him and solemnly swears to carry him out of Egypt to the grave of his fathers, and Jacob bows in worship at the bed's head.

Seen from across the courtyard under the high midday sun, Joseph's chariot draws up at his father's house among the palms and pastures of Goshen, and Joseph walks in with his two sons, the youths Manasseh and Ephraim; through the wide doorway, servants help Jacob, who has heard of his coming, to sit up on his bed to receive them.

In the quiet bedchamber in the late afternoon, Jacob sits up on his bed with one hand raised, telling Joseph how God Almighty appeared to him at Luz, and how Rachel died on the road to Bethlehem; Joseph sits listening beside the bed, Manasseh and Ephraim stand near the door, and low sunlight slants through a window over the palms.

By lamplight, Jacob, his eyes dim with age, reaches out from his bed as Joseph brings his two sons near; he draws the youths into his arms and kisses them, overjoyed to see Joseph's children, while Joseph bows himself with his face to the floor beside the bed, and the household watches quietly from the doorway.

Seen from across the morning-lit room, Joseph sets Ephraim before his father's left hand and Manasseh before his right, but Jacob deliberately crosses his arms, laying his right hand on the younger Ephraim's head and his left on Manasseh's, and blesses them in the name of the God of his fathers, while the room falls hushed.

Seen from the foot of the bed in warm afternoon light, Joseph, displeased, takes hold of his father's right hand to move it onto Manasseh's head, but Jacob gently refuses, keeping it on Ephraim and saying the younger shall be greater; the two youths kneel side by side before the bed, while servants look on from the doorway.

At sunset, with the last red light glowing through the open doorway and the pastures of Goshen beyond, Jacob holds Joseph's hand on the bed and tells him he is dying, but God will bring them back to the land of their fathers; Joseph kneels close, and his two sons stand behind him in the deepening shadows.

In a large room open to the green fields of Goshen, in soft morning light, Jacob sits up on his bed as his twelve sons gather around him in a wide half-circle; Reuben, the firstborn, stands before him with his head bowed as his father speaks of his strength and his failing, and the other brothers watch solemnly.

Seen from the doorway on a cold, overcast day, Jacob turns his face away and raises a hand in rebuke toward two brothers, Simeon and Levi, who stand before the bed with lowered heads and hanging arms, reminded of their fierce anger; the other brothers look on uneasily as clouds pass over the sun and shadow fills the room.

A vision of Jacob's blessing: Judah stands on a rocky height at sunrise holding a royal sceptre, a great lion resting on the rocks at his feet; below him spread rich terraced vineyards heavy with purple grapes, where a young donkey is tied to a choice vine, and his brothers bow toward him from the slope below.

A wide landscape of Jacob's blessing in bright midday sun: on one side a sheltered harbour where ships ride at anchor and fishermen haul nets onto the shore; on the other a pleasant green valley where a strong donkey lies resting between two heavy loads, and farmers bend their shoulders under burdens in the golden fields.

column4: Dan, a serpent by the way
column7: On a narrow mountain path at dusk, a horned viper coiled beside the track strikes at the heels of a horse, which rears up as its rider is thrown backward; far below in the valley, a judge sits at a town gate among the people of Dan, and the first evening star shines in the fading sky, as if waiting for deliverance.

Seen from a hilltop in the morning sun, green hill country spreads out: a graceful hind bounds free across a flowering meadow; in the valley below, Asher's rich fields surround a village where ovens bake fine bread for royal tables, and on a far ridge Gad's men stand firm, driving off a band of raiders who flee into the distance.

In a vision of Jacob's blessing, a great vine heavy with fruit grows beside an old stone well and spreads its branches up and over a high wall; Joseph stands beneath it, steadfast, while far off on a dry ridge a band of archers lower their bows, and warm afternoon light bathes the everlasting hills that roll away behind him.

Seen from above, back in the bedchamber on a quiet, rainy afternoon, Jacob lays his hand on Benjamin, the youngest, who kneels before him as the last to be blessed; the other eleven sons stand around the bed in a full circle, each one blessed, while beyond the wide doorway a soft rain falls on the pastures of Goshen.

At sunset the room glows red and gold; Jacob, lying back on his bed, gives his sons his last charge to bury him with his fathers in the cave of Machpelah, then draws his feet up into the bed and breathes his last in peace, as his twelve sons bow their heads around him and the first lamps flicker in the dusk.

In a lamp-lit chamber in the grey before dawn, Joseph kneels weeping beside his father, who lies still on his bed as if asleep; Egyptian physicians wait respectfully nearby with linen wrappings and jars of spices to embalm him, and in the courtyard beyond, a crowd of Egyptian mourners stands with bowed heads.

Seen from high in Pharaoh's columned audience hall in the bright midday light, Joseph, in plain mourning garments, stands before the throne asking leave to go up and bury his father in Canaan as he swore; Pharaoh lifts his hand and nods his consent, and the officials lining the hall look on with sympathy.

An aerial view of a vast funeral procession winding out of Egypt across the golden desert in the early morning: chariots and horsemen ride ahead and behind, Pharaoh's elders and officials walk in white robes, and in the middle Joseph and his brothers walk beside Jacob's coffin, borne on poles and draped in fine cloth, as dust rises into the sky.

On a wide stone threshing floor atop a hill beyond the Jordan, under a heavy grey sky, the great company sits in sackcloth and dust around Jacob's draped coffin, lamenting loudly for seven days; Canaanite villagers watch in wonder from the neighbouring hillside, and the green river valley stretches away below.

In the late afternoon, beneath the great oaks of Mamre, Jacob's sons carry his coffin on their shoulders toward the dark mouth of the cave of Machpelah, cut into a rocky hillside at the end of a field of olive trees; Joseph leads them, while the chariots and Egyptian mourners wait respectfully in the field, ready to return to Egypt.

At ground level in the courtyard of Joseph's house in soft morning light, his brothers fall on their faces on the paved floor before him, begging forgiveness and offering themselves as his servants; Joseph stands among the potted palms weeping at their fear, while the messenger who carried their plea waits quietly beside the gate.

Seen from above in the sunny courtyard, Joseph stoops to raise his brothers to their feet, one hand on Judah's shoulder and the other reaching out to the rest, telling them not to fear, for God meant their evil for good; the brothers' faces ease into relief and tears, and their children watch from the shade of the colonnade.

In a garden by the Nile in the golden afternoon, Joseph, now very old, sits in a carved chair beneath a spreading sycamore fig with his great-grandchildren, the children of Ephraim's line and of Machir, on his knees and playing at his feet; their parents gather around him smiling, and the river shines beyond the palms.

At dusk in a quiet chamber, Joseph lies on his bed and lifts his hand as his brothers and the gathered children of Israel solemnly swear to carry his bones up to the land promised to their fathers; beyond the open portico the Nile glows in the last light, and a plain, unmarked coffin waits in the shadows.
